speakeroldname: Mr. F. B. CARVELL (Carleton, N.B.) moved:
speechtext:
For a copy of all letters, telegrams, correspondence and contracts between the Department of Railways and Canals or any official thereof, including the officials of the Intercolonial railway, and any member of the Government of New Brunswick, the St. John and Quebec Railway Company or any official thereof, regarding the operation of the Valley Railway, so-called, in the province of New Brunswick, from the first day of October, 1914, down to the present date.
He said: This motion refers to a subject which has been debated in this House on a number of occasions during the last four or five years, but I think there has been no occasion on which it was fraught with so much importance to the people of my province as it is to-day. I am sorry to say it has been made a political football by my hon. friends opposite and their friends in the province of New Brunswick for the past six years, and now we have reached a stage in the history of the transaction which, 1 think, calls for a frank and open statement, on behalf of this Government, for the information of the people of New Bruns-

wick, who have incurred a liability of about $5,000,000, or who, purely on account of the * promise given by the Federal Government and the Federal Parliament, will have incurred a liability greater than that before the transaction is completed.
I am not going into the history of this matter to any very great extent because it has been discussed in this House on a great many occasions, and tRe condition existing is of much greater importance than the history of it. Suffice it to say, that away back in 1909 or 1910, an agitation was started in the province of New Brunswick to construct a railroad from the Transcontinental railway at Grand Falls to the city of St. John. The proposition first came from the present Minister of Marine and Fisheries who, at that time, was Premier of New Brunswick and it was that if the Dominion Government would operate this railway as part of the Intercolonial system on a 40 per cent basis, that is, by paying to the Goverment of New Brunswick 40 per cent of the gross earnings with which to secure the interest on the bonds, they would guarantee the bonds. The matter was put up to the then Government, and I think I ought to be frank enough to say that the authorities of the Intercolonial Railway objected very seriously to the proposition. They took the . ground that it was a much better proposition for the province of New Brunswick than for the Intercolonial Railway. However, it was discussed on many occasions; large delegations came from New Brunswick and we were able to convince the Prime Minister and the then Minister of Railways, and the Government generally, that it was a proposition which had merit, and which should be accepted officially. The proposition was accepted, and legislation was passed in the year 1911. It will be found as chapter 11 of the statutes of that year, and as it is very short, I shall read the whole chapter.
The Governor in Council is authorized to enter into a contract with any railway company already authorized, or which may be hereafter authorized by law, to construct a line of railway from a point on the line of the National Transcontinental railway at Grand Falls, in the county of Victoria, to the city of St. John, in the province of New Brunswick, a distance of about two 'hundred and twenty miles, the principal and interest of the bonds of which railway company, pursuant to' the provisions of chapter 6, of the statutes of the province of New Brunswick, 1910, the Government of the province of New Brunswick has guaranteed, or may guarantee, to the extent of twenty-five thousand [DOT] dollars per mile, and with the Government of the province of New Brunswick, for the leasing of the said line of railway when completed, with
its appurtenances, and for its operation, equipment, maintenance, upkeep and repair by the Government of Canada, as part of the Govem-mentment Railway system of Canada, for a period of ninety-nine years and for the payment by the Government of Canada to the said province of New Brunswick, or to the said company, each year during the said term of ninety-nine years, of forty per centum of the gross earnings of the said railway as or in the nature of rental thereof:	Provided, however, that the said contract shall be entered into only upon the condition that the said railway be constructed upon plans and specifications to be approved of by the Governor in Council upon the recommendation of the Minister of Railways and Canals, and shall be up to the general standard of the said National Transcontinental railway through the said province; provided further that the Governor in Council shall be authorized to enter into a contract, as aforesaid, for the operation of the said railway in sections, when completed and equipped as follows:
(1)	From Fredericton to Woodstock;
(2)	From Fredericton, south, 'a distance of forty miles ;
(3)	Each twenty-five miles thereafter, until the line be completed from Grand Falls to St. John.
The remaining section has reference only to the directors. That Act was passed, I think, in the month of March, 1911, and the General .Elections took place in September, 1911, which resulted in a change of Government. Almost immediately thereafter an arrangement was entered into between the present Government and the Government of New Brunswick for the construction of this road. They changed the legislation in many material respects, but I do not intend to spend very much time over that. The new arrangement was entered into in 1912, and it will be found in chapter 49 of the statutes of that year, the substantive part of the statute reviving an agreement previously made between the Government of New Brunswick and tiie Government of Canada. I wish to read from section 3 of the agreement, because that is the portion of the statute which made the agreement between the two parties, which we in New Brunswick believed they intended to carry out, and in regard to which we are finding a great deal of fault because it has not been carried out. It reads:
The Dominion hereby undertakes and agrees that as soon as the said railway is constructed and equipped to the satisfaction of the engineer or engineers so appointed as aforesaid, between Fredericton and Woodstock, the Dominion will enter into a lease in accordance with the terms and conditions herein agreed upon and to bS embodied in the said lease, and that when a further section of the said railway from Fredericton southwards towards Saint John, a distance of forty miles, shall have been constructed and equipped to the satisfaction of such engineer or engineers, the Dominion will enter into a lease thereof and operate upon like terms

and conditions as above mentioned and so on thereafter as each section of twenty-five miles of railway is constructed and equipped, the Dominion will enter into a lease thereof and operate in manner afore mentioned, and when the said whole line between Saint John and Grand Falls is fully constructed and equipped, the Dominion will lease the said line including the said bridges upon like terms and conditions for the term of ninety-nine years, it being understood and agreed that the Dominion will provide the necessary, suitable and sufficient rolling stock for the operation of the said railway and will maintain, repair and upkeep the said railway at its own expense during the whole term of the lease, such lease to contain all the usual and necessary covenants, provisoes and conditions, and the company hereby covenants and agrees to grant the said leases accordingly.	. .	, ,,
Provided, however, that the Dominion shall not be required to enter into any lease of any constructed and equipped section of the said railway which is not connected with the completed" and equipped railway from Fredericton so as to form a continuous line of railway.
I have taken some time to read that to the House, but in order to make it thoroughly plain and understandable, it is necessary to give some information as to the history of the legislation in connection with this undertaking. The (old Government passed a law providing for the operation by the Intercolonial railway of this road, when constructed. When the present Government came into power, they changed the thing, not to a very great extent, but providing also for the operation of this road by the Intercolonial, paying to the province of New Brunswick 40 per cent of the gross earnings therof, and providing also, as plain as the English language could provide, that they would enter into a lease for the operation of this road in sections as soon as each individual section was completed. The first section was to be from Fredericton to Woodstock, 62 miles, the second from Fredericton south 40 miles, and it was provided that whenever 25 miles were completed it should become a new section which the Federal Government agreed to lease and operate on these conditions. 'In order to understand the matter thoroughly it will be necessary to keep that in mind because that is the very important thing which the present Government or the present Intercolonial management, have neglected or refused to do. It is almost impossible to find out either from the Federal authorities, or from the province of New Brunswick, whether any such lease was ever entered into. I may say that my impression is, from my reading and from [DOT].asking questions-and I have asked a great .many of them both here and in New 
Brunswick-(that	no such lease has
ever been entered into although the Intercolonial Railway, as a matter of fact, has been operating certain portions of this road since about the first of January, 1915.
There is another statute referring to it which I also wish to cite 'because it plays a very important part in the matter. It is chapter 52 of the statutes of 1914. In order to carry out this work, as it was provided for, that is the road from Grand Falls to St. John, it was necessay to build three important bridges across the river St. John. The first would be at Andover in Victoria county. That bridge would not involve any very serious difficulties because the river is, I suppose, 500 or 600 feet wide, *with high banks and a hard bottom and this would simply he an ordinary piece of railway bridge construction. Two other bridges would he necessary, one across the St. John river, probably 50 miles below Fredericton or in that vicinity, and another across the Kennebecasis river a few miles from Rothesay. We do not deny that thdse are expensive bridges, but we would like to know what the Government has done, and further, we would like to find out the position of affairs, not the exact, but the probable, cost of these bridges, and the engineering difficulties, "if any there "be, in the way of carrying out the arrangement. Let that be as it may, in 1914, the Minister of Railways and Canals brought a Bill before this Parliament providing for assistance to the St. John and Quebec Railway Company for the construction of these bridges. You may remember that during that year there was quite a stir in political affairs in the province of New Brunswick over the construction of this Valley railway. Certain charges of a very grave character were preferred against members of the Provincial Government by one of the members of the Legislature. These charges were referred to a Royal Commission which investigated the matter very thoroughly and which found that certain irregularities had occurred; that the contractors had paid money to the then Premier; that something like $450,000 or $600,000 'had been added to the cost of this road improperly without authority, and for which they would have received Government bonds of the province of New Brunswick giving no returns for them had it not been for that investigation. I am not going into the details of it because it does not affect this Parliament to any great extent. It was, however, a pretty rotten mess. I was a little suspicious

about granting any further aid to the St. John and Quebec Railway Company, and I protested as vigorously as I knew how against granting any further aid to this company or to any subsidiary company for the construction of these bridges. After about three or four weeks, the Government announced that they would build these bridges themselves and if any hon. gentleman will look up Hansard he will find that I heartily commended the Minister of Railways and Canals. I told him that I believed that his department would be honest, and that these bridges would be built properly, and that both the Dominion of Canada and the province of New Brunswick would get the accommodation to which they were entitled. I shall not read the whole statute although there are only four sections in it; the important section is section 1:
The Governor in Council may build the said three railway bridges including all necessary approaches and appurtenances; and the said bridges, approaches and appurtenances shall belong to and be the property of His Majesty.
The second section provides that the minister may enter into an agreement with the Government of New Brunswick and the St. John and Quebec Railway Company for the operation of these bridges and that for the first fifteen years the province of New Brunswick and the Tailway company were to pay nothing in so far as these bridges were concerned. After the expiration of the fifteen years they were to pay a certain proportion of the earnings, but that is not very particular. The main thing is that this Parliament authorized the Minister of Railways and Canals, and this Government, to build these three bridges and we believed in the province of New Brunswick and I am of the opinion that Parliament and the Government did believe it, that it was the intention to have them constructed, and that would end the troubles which have been so rampant in New Brunswick for the last four or five years over this railway matter. I always had some doubts about the bona fides of the Government of New Brunswick with regard to this transaction. I do not go so far as to say I have any doubts . about the bona fides of this Government; in fact, I would almost take the opposite view. I believe that the great majority of the members of this Government were absolutely bona fide in what they were doing. I believe that they intended to operate that road when constructed
and I believe they intended to build these bridges. But the tempter has been at work very assiduously for the last three or four years and something has happened. What has happened is the very thing that I would like to find out and that is my object in discussing this motion to-day. I only wish that the Minister of Railways and Canals had been here to give us the real history of the transaction and tell us exactly what has taken place. Somehow or other there has always been a feeling in New Brunswick from the beginning, or rather from the year 1910, that the Government of New Brunswick were not sincere in the professions, in the legislation, in the contracts and in the things which they were doing regarding this Valley railway question. That is a very harsh statement to make but I know that I am voicing the sentiments of every Liberal in New Brunswick and I think I am voicing the sentiments of three-quarters of the Conservatives of that province, when I make that statement. We have always said that there was something about this that was not straight, manly and upright; that something was being held back, and that the people had been deluded and deceived from the very beginning. Those sentiments have been voiced in this House by myself and my colleagues on at least one, I should think a dozen different occasions. The Minister of Railways (Mr. Cochrane) and I have discu'ssed this matter on many occasions in this House. I have also discussed it with my hon. friend the Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Mr. Hazen), who I notice is conveniently absent to-day. I voiced my sentiments to him in the House, and I have his pledge on Hansard in language as strong as he could possibly make it. We discussed this matter first in the House in 1912, on an amendment proposed by my hon. friend the member for Victoria and Madawaska. Before the old Government went out of power a subsidy had been voted for the building of this road from Grand Falls to St. John, and in 1912, when the subsidy was being renewed, this Government dropped off the twenty-five miles from Andover to the Transcontinental, and renewed the subsidy only from Andover to St. John. That looked very suspicious to us at the time, and we did not hesitate to say so, and practically every hon. member from New Brunswick in the House at that time spoke in the debate. We discussed it in all its moods and tenses, and told this Government that we did not think they were sincere

when they dropped that portion of the subsidy from Andover to the Transcontinental. I should like to read a portion of the discussion I had at that time with the Minister of Railways, and which is found on page 6384 of Hansard, March 28, 1911-12. After pointing out my fears with regard to the dropping of this portion of the subsidy, and saying that I did not believe they intended to carry out their pledges, I used these words:
Do you wonder that we are a little suspicious and a little in fear that the declarations of the intentions of the railway company and the declarations of the intentions of the government of New Brunswick up to last May will be carried out.
Mr. Cochrane : Have no fear.
Mr. Carvell: We have our fears.
Mr. Cochrane: Have faith.
Mr. Carvell: Perhaps, if my hon, friend knew as much about this matter as we do, he would not have as much faith as he has at the present time. It is in order to ensure the construction of this road and to put it beyond perad-venture, that I am supporting this amendment. We believe that if they are allowed to go on as they are doing, nothwithstanding the good intentions of my hon. friend, the Minister ot Railways and Canals the results may not be satisfactory. I give my hon. friend credit for having good intentions, hut he is not above temptation and I can assure him that the tempter will be so strong, that I do not believe that he, even with his forcible character, will be able to withstand him, and it is in order to remove my hon. friend from danger of that temptation, that I support this amendment.
Then, on page 6387-8, the Minister of Marine and Fisheries, after referring to these very remarks of mine, used the following language:
Now, coming to the really important question involved in this, as to the road going to Grand Falls, I am as certain as I am standing here that the road is going to Grand Falls, and I do not believe there is a particle of doubt in the mind of the government of New Brunswick but that that road is going to Grand Falls. The subsidy is voted for a road to Grand Falls, and the Government is authorized to operate the road from Grand Falls to the city of St. John, and the contract entered into in specific terms sets out that such will be the fact. The Minister of Railways has arranged the terms of the contract with the representatives of the government of New Brunswick and the company, and my hon. friend the minister will have no hesitation in telling the House that that road will be operated and built from Grand Falls to the city of St. John, and neither the New Brunswick government nor this government could tolerate for a moment a condition of affairs under which the road would be built to Andover and suddenly stop therewithout having the advantage of a connection with the Transcontinental at some point in the county of Victoria at or near the village of Grand Falls.
If it were possible for a stronger statement to have been made by a minister of the Crown, who also happened to be the

former Premier of New Brunswick who had launched this proposition, I should like to know what stronger language he could have used. It may surprise you, Mr. Speaker, that even after that forcible declaration by the Minister of Marine and Fisheries there were dpubting Thomases in New Brunswick, who did not believe that the Government of the province of New Brunswick would carry out their pledges. I do not by any means say that the Minister of Marine and Fisheries was deceiving the House, but we had not faith in the Government of New Brunswick. That was be* fore the explosion took place in 1914, but -we knew just who they were almost as well before the explosion as after, only they were not exposed to 1jiie public till 1914.
Then they were caught with the goods.

From the beginning of this railway project there was nothing but insincerity, delusion, and deceit on the part of the Government of New Brunswick as to what they were going to do and what; they were not going to do with regard to the construction of this important railway. I have one more citation to make before leaving that branch of the ease, and it is from the remarks of the Minister of Marine and Fisheries in the discussion that we had in the House with reference to the offer of this Government to build the bridges to which I made reference some time ago. You will find these remarks in Hansard of April 28, 1914, page 3018. Mind you, two years had gone by since the declaration of the Minister of Marine and Fisheries that this road would be built to Grand Falls; two years after he had used the words I have already quoted, namely:
Neither the New Brunswick government nor this government could tolerate for a moment a condition of affairs under which the road would he built to Andover and suddenly stop there without having the advantage of a connection with the Transcontinental at some point in the county of Victoria at or near the village of Grand Falls.
Two years had gone by. The province of New Brunswick, acting through the St. John and Quebec Railway Company, had commenced the construction of the road, and had partially constructed, about 120 miles of it. But still we did not believe that they were sincere. Coming back to this House after the charges had been laid in the Provincial Legislature, I again stated that I did not believe the Government of New Brunswick were sincere and intended to

build, the road through to the Transcontinental, and the Minister of Marine and Fisheries then used these words (page 3018):
The speech of the hon. member for Carleton might be read in two ways. To a certain class it could be said: The hon. member for Carleton is entirely, opposed to having these bridges built at all. Is the hon. gentleman sincere and candid in the statements which he has made to the House to-day? Is the hon. gentleman not still playing the game that he has played for so many years of trying to prevent the Government from coming to the aid of this road, and to the aid of the province and making provision by which these bridges shall be built and without which the rest of the road is an impossibility? The hon. gentleman has also referred to the question of the connection at Grand Falls. There is no doubt in the world that there will be connection at Grand Falls with the St. John Valley railway. The only doubt about the matter in the mind of the Minister of Railways and Canals is whether it will be necessary to build a bridge across the river and to build twenty-five or thirty miles of railway, or whether the same result can be attained without any such expenditure by obtaining running rights from Andover to Grand Falls over the existing line of railway and which, in large measure, would be paralleled if a new line were built. A year ago there was no doubt, and there is no doubt today, but that the railway known as the St. John Valley will connect at Grand Falls with the Grand Trunk Pacific and be in a position to receive from that railway western freight at Grand Falls to be hauled over the road and shipped out of the port of St. John, and also to carry freight from the port of St. John to Grand Falls.
There, again, Sir, you have the same positive, explicit declaration on the part of the Minister of Marine and Fisheries that this road would go to Grand Falls, but there was just this little difference: Two years had rather undermined the hon. gentleman's assurance because, while in 1912 there was not a particle of doubt that the road was going straight through to Grand Falls and connect with the Transcontinental, in 1914, a little doubt had ecme over the hon. gentleman's mind because he was not sure whether it would be better to construct a new road crossing the river at Andover or to utilize the Canadian Pacific railway tracks from Perth or Andover up to Grand Falls; but the one or the other would happen without the shadow of a doubt, and I was chided, as I have been chided by my hon. friend for the last five years, and the people of New Brunswick were told, as they had been told for two years before that, that I was trying to throw every possible obstacle in the way, but that, with all my obstruction and with all the obstacles that I was putting in the way of the Government of Canada, they would persevere to the end; they would
build that road; they would build those bridges; they would make the connection and they would give to the people of New Brunswick that which they had promised. them.
This story has been told in this House, in the New 'Brunswick Legislature, on the hustings of New Brunswick and in every Tory paper for so long that one would almost be forced to believe that Carvel] and Pugsley had horns and hoofs; that they did not belong to the human species; that they existed only for the purpose of preventing the construction of this road and preventing the Government at Ottawa from working out the greatest good to the greatest number of people in New Brunswick. But a great deal is to be said for the prophesies of Carvell and Pugsley and for the way in which they were able to foresee what would happen. We had no faith in the men who had charge of the matter; we did not believe they were sincere or honest; we do not believe now they are sincere or honest. The events of the last three weeks have justified our prophesies and our fears to a greater extent than have the fears of any member of this House been justified in the last quarter of a century. In the first place, the construction of this road was never justified; the province of Ntew Brunswick was never justified in putting a dollar into it nor in guaranteeing a dollar of bonds unless the original arrangement had been carried out to the letter, unless this road had gone through to Grand Falls or some other point on the Transcontinental. My own judgment is that Grand Falls is the proper point, but the road must make connection with the Transcontinental in the neighbourhood of Grand Falls in order to get through business, and, without that through business, this railway is one of the greatest political crimes that has ever been foisted upon a free country, the crime of spending over $4,000,000 of our money, and of giving us nothing but a load of debt around our shoulders in the end.
I do not mean to say that this road is not a great advantage to the country through which it passes. It is a great local advantage, but we forced the Government to build a pretty good railroad; in fact, the mechanical portion of the road, outside of the curves and grades, is very good and the expenditure of a little more money on straightening out curves and eliminating grades would make the road a very good one. But the idea of putting on the province of New Brunswick a debt which will amount to $5,000,000 when the road is completed,

and of not carrying out the general scheme , of connecting it with the Transcontinental where through business could be obtained, is unjustified from the standpoint both of the province and of the Dominion.
Under the arrangement, as I have read it from the statutes of 1911 and 1912, the Intercolonial Railway or the Government of Canada was to lease this road and to operate it, in sections at first, and as .a completed road, when it was completed, and forty cents of every dollar earned were to go back to the province. We argued that in New Brunswick and our opponents did the same, and the people of New Brunswick finally agreed to the proposition on the distinct understanding that forty per cent of the revenue of that road would go to pay the interest on the bonds, and I have no doubt that, if this road went through to Grand Palls and to St. John and made the through connection as proposed, in a short time 40 per cent of the gross earnings would be enough to pay the interest on the bonds. But instead of building the road to Grand Falls; instead of building it even to Andover and taking running rights over the Canadian Pacific railway to Grand Falls, they have built it to a place called Centreville in my constituency twenty-five miles from Andover, and there they have stopped, and it has been announced in papers supporting the Government that it is not the Government's policy to contract the railway further. They are breaking faith with a very large section of the people of the province as individuals, and they are breaking faith with the whole province collectively, because they ^re stopping just when they are in sight of that point at which they could carry on a profitable business not only for the Intercolonial Railway, but for the province of New Brunswick, and that is our greatest concern at the present time.
At the beginning of this session I asked a number of questions of the Minister of Railways, and on the 14th of February I received answers to them. I wish to read the questions and answers, which will be found on page 757 of this year's Hansard:
Mr. Carvell:
1.	What amount of money has been paid by the Intercolonial railway or the Government of Canada to the government of New Brunswick as their proportion of the earnings of the Valley railway, so-called, down to December 31 last?
Mr. Cochrane:
1,	None, but there is due to the "province of New Brunswick, under the arrangement whereby

the province was to receive 40 per cent of the gross receipts, $18,733.65, accruing during the nine months ended December 31.
Question:
2.	Has the province of New Brunswick received 40 per cent of the gross earnings of said railway since the beginning of its operation? If not, what percentage of said earnings has the province received?
Answer:
2.	No. From the commencement of operation, January 1, 1915, until March 31, 1915, the arrangement was, that the provinces and the Dominion each should bear one-half of the deficit, if any. Under this arrangement, the province owes the Dominion $2,977.51.
Question:
3.	Was an agreement signed between the two governments around the first of January, 1915, or shortly thereafter, for the operation of the said railway on what is known as the 40 per cent basis?
Answer:	.
3.	There was no formal agreement.
Question:
4.	Has a new agreement been entered into between the two governments within the last month or six weeks as to the operation of the said road and the distribution of the earnings thereof?
Answer:
4.	No.
Question:
5.	Under said new agreement what proportion of the gross earnings are payable to the province of New Brunswick?
Answer:
5.	Answered by No. 4.
Question:
6.	Did the Department of Railways and
Canals in the month of December last order the cessation of the operation of the said road to take effect on the 1st day of January instant?
Answer:
6.	Ordered cessation of the temporary arrangement which led to negotiations which resulted in the order to continue operation after January 1, 1916, on terms to be arranged.
Question:
7.	If so, what were the reasons for such order?
Answer:
7.	The non-completion of the road.
Now, Sir, you will bear in mind that I read from the statutes of 1911 and 1912 that the road was to be operated in sections; that, as each section was completed, it was to be operated. The road from Fredericton to Woodstock was completed before January, 1915. The road from Woodstock north for twenty-five miles, which would make

one section, was completed and was in operation before 1st January, 1915. The roach from Fredericton south, the next section, which, under the statute, should have been forty miles, I confess, was only carried to the length of thirty-six or thirty-seven miles. That length of construction brought the railway to Gagetown, a bright little town, the shire town of the county of Queens, quite a large centre. And- would you believe it, Mr. Speaker-the Department of Railways of this Government absolutely refused to run a train over that road for nearly a year, on the ground, as they said, that it had not been completed for forty miles, and so did not comply with the agreement. Here was a road which had cost from $38,000 to $40,000 a mile, completed even to the station-houses and the stoves in them, and yet, because it was only thirty-six or thirty-seven miles long, instead, of forty miles long, they said it was not completed and they would not carry it on. But they could not use that argument as to the portion north of Fredericton, for it was completed. I do not say "completed" in the sense that an engineer going over it could say that there was not another spike to be driven. In that sense a railway is never completed,. An engineer might go over the Grand Trunk from Montreal to Toronto, the finest piece of road in the country, and find a tie here and there to be replaced, or some other little thing to be done, because of which he might report the road as not completed. But to all practical purposes this road was completed north of Fredericton, and it was completed south of Fredericton. They never signed the agreement which they had covenanted to sign, and on the strength of which covenant the people of New Brunswick had voted for the present Provincial Government in the elections of 1912, so that the Government carried every county in New Brunswick except one, and to-day have the support of every member of the legislature save two, the voting being on the pledge that they would complete this valley railway from Grand Falls to St. John, and on the pledge of the Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Mr. Hazen) in this House, which I have read this afternoon, given only two or three months before the elections, that this Government would take the road over and operate it by sections as completed and finally the completed road, and that this Government would see that the road was completed from Grand Falls, and would build these bridges-no, I am wrong, for that legislation was after the election; but
there was legislation in 1912 providing for $1,000,000 to assist toward the building of these bridges. So, when the people of New Brunswick voted confidence in the Provincial Government, as they did in every county save one, they did it on the express covenant of this Government that they would build these bridges, or would see to it that they were built, and that the road should be operated, and the province of New Brunswick should be given 40 per cent of the gross earnings to pay the interest on the bonds.
When the road had been in operation for a year, that is, from 1st January, 1915, to 31st December, 1915, instead of entering into a lease as they had agreed, they signed no lease. They had run a very indifferent service, simply a combination passenger and freight train from. Fredericton to Centreville and back once a day. On the lower end, from Fredericton to Gagetown, they had run no trains. Last summer they arranged for a train a week, and that service continued up to Christmas. Now, I think, they are running two or three trains a week from Fredericton south. But they never signed the agreement, and never made themselves liable to pay to the province the 40 per cent, and they have not paid that 40 per cent, nor 30 per cent, nor 20 per cent, nor one per cent. The Intercolonial has been operating that road and taking the receipts, and we poor people in New Brunswick are paying interest on $4,000,000 of bonds, while they are getting all the benefit. They admit, however, that under the "arrangement," as they call it, there would have been about $18,733 due to the province last December.
As if that were not bad enough, two days after Christmas every employee on the road received notice that his services would be dispensed with on January 31. Hundreds of tons of freight had been hauled to the different stations of the railway to be shipped, and business was going on. There was a pretty lively time for a while and the wires were kept busy. I do not know what was done, but such a row was raised that the Intercolonial authorities were afraid to carry out their threat, and on the morning of the 30th or 31st December the order cancelling the trains was itself cancelled and the .arrangement went on as in the past. But they say in their answer to me that they agreed to continue it on terms to be arranged later on. And the object I had in discussing this question to-day was to find out what terms had been arranged on which they are going to carry on this work. It is

important in the interest of the province that that should he made clear. In the first place, we know that the province of New Brunswick had guaranteed bonds to the extent of close upon $6,000,000. Possibly I may be a little in error in that, but I will explain the exact conditions so far as we know them. We know that away back in 1912 they guaranteed bonds to the extent of $25,000 a mile for 170 miles, a total of something over $4,000,000. These bonds were sold in London and the money was brought back here before the elections of 1912 and placed in the hands of the Prudential Trust Company, of Montreal, the trustees under the agreement between the Government of New Brunswick and the railway company. The company paid out the money on progress estimates by the chief engineer of the road. When we got through our investigation in the autumn of 1914, there was $1,000,000, in round figures, in the hands of the Prudential Trust Company. I learn, by an answer given in the New Brunswick Legislature on Friday last, that something like $700,000 of this money is still in the hands of the company for constructive purposes. But they claim that they had advanced a portion to the Government, which would mean that something like $400,000 of this money would be in the hands of the Government. In addition to nearly $700,000 or $684,000 to be more exact-there is about $170,000 in their hands for the payment of interest on the bonds. So, we have $850,000 anyway of the proceeds of these bonds supposed to be in the hands of the Prudential Trust Company in Montreal. I have discussed that before in the House and have nothing more to say about it. We in New Brunswick sincerely trust, and almost pray, that when the time comes for the company to be called upon for this money, it will be forthcoming. Further than that, we do not go at this time.
We do know, however, that during the whole of the last session of the legislature in New Brunswick the Opposition attempted to get from the Government a statement with Tegard to the money that had been deposited with the Prudential Trust Company. We were told that they had securities running up to about $2,000,000 repre- * senting the investment, but they positively refused to give us a list of those securities. No one in the province of New Brunswick to-day, outside of the members of the Government, have the faintest idea how or when or where or under what conditions this enormous amount of money is invest-

ed. We do know that the Government also guaranteed second mortgage bonds to the extent of $10,000 a mile. Whether they guaranteed the whole 170 miles or only the 120 I do not know. It may be that they guaranteed only 120, because while they have guaranteed 170 miles of bonds of the first mortgage issue, they havg built only 120 miles of road. Every bond for the 170 miles was sold in London in the month of May, 1912, and the proceeds were brought back to Canada and deposited with the Prudential Trust Company. You will see, Sir, that the province of New Brunswick has guaranteed bonds in this matter to the extent of about $6,000,000. $4,000,000 of this were at 4 per cent; the rest at 5 or better than 5 per cent. I think we would be safe in saying that the average rate would be ii per cent, which would be $240,000 or $250,000 a year for which the province of New Brunswick is liable in respect of this railway transaction. We went into this enormous undertaking and we guaranteed these bonds, on the strength of the covenant of this Government, the Minister of Railways and Canals and this Parliament, that these bridges would be built, that the road would go through to Grand Falls, tap the Transcontinental and become a portion of the through line. On the strength of that agreement we belived that 40 per cent of the gross earnings would be sufficient to pay the interest on those bonds. If these conditions are not carried out, and if the road does not become the business proposition that we were led to believe it would become-and which we know it would become if the conditions were carried out- the province of New Brunswick will become liable to an annual outlay of $225,000 or $250,000, less, of course, the small amount that might be raised from the operation of the road as the Government evidently intend to operate it under present conditions. As at present constructed, the road is merely an ordinary branch line of the Canadian Pacific railway. Twenty-five miles below Centreville, which is now its terminus, the road crosses the Canadian Pacific railway. If a car of freight is going to the United States market, it leaves the road at that point and goes by the Canadian Pacific railway. As it is about 450 miles from Centreville to Boston, which is the distributing point of all freight from New Brunswick to the United States, the amount which this road would receive for carrving the freight over that 25 miles would be merely a shunting charge. The amount received for carry-

ing a car of freight would be so small as to be hardly worth considering, and 40 per cent of the gross earnings would be a more bagatelle. If you had 10,000 cars a year going over that road, you would hardly see what it would amount to in the end. Again, the line goes south to Woodstock for a distance of 25 or 30 miles, picks up the goods and either brings them to Woodstock and hands them over to the Canadian Pacilc railway, or carries them to Fredericton and hands them over to the Canadian Pacific railroad. No matter which way you go, under present conditions this Toad, so far as constructed, is simply a feeder or a series of feeders for the great Canadian Pacific railway system.
'I now come to the propositions which are on foot in the province of New Brunswick, and which, I presume, are the terms arranged between the Government of New Brunswick and this Government. I know that a delegation from the Government of New Brunswick was here last week or the week before, just before the provincial legislature met. They had several conferences with the	Minister	of Marine and
Fisheries, the Minister of Railways, and, I assume, with the Government. Evidently they came to some sort of agreement, because they went home called together the legislature, and, in the Speech from the Throne, stated that legislation would be introduced to provide for the completion of the Valley railway. The Government have announced that they will not build this road north of Centreville; so far as that end of the line is concerned, it is finished, and there is no possible connection with the Grand Trunk Pacific railway. So far as the lower end is concerned, instead of building the bridges which this Government covenanted they would build, they say:	Oh, well, an investigation was
made by an engineer by the name of Mon-sarrat. This gentleman, who, I believe, is an engineer of repute, reported that the' construction of these bridges would cost an enormous amount of money, and that there was a poor bottom. I am told-and I believe that I am stating the facts-that Mr. Mon-sarrat never made a boring in his life in the St. John River, and does not know anything about it; that he took the data given him by somebody else, and said that if those data were correct, he did not believe that these undertakings were feasible. I have no doubt that, as an engineering proposition, taking the data as given to Mr. Monsarrat, the conclusion that he arrived at was justifiable. I am not going to reveal confidences, but I want to tell the Government of New Brunswick that if they will produce a report made to them by their own chief engineer within the last three months, they will find that this is a practicable proposition, and that none of the bugaboos and quagmires and fanciful difficulties exist which they say exist. This excuse is only a scheme to get around carrying out their contract with the people of New Brunswick, to get this Government rid of carrying out its contract and to get 5 p.m. the Intercolonial rid of carrying out its contract. If they will let us examine Mr. Maxwell for ten minutes, I know what his statement will be. They may have compelled the man to put something) in a report, perhaps, but if we had a chance to cross-examine Mr. Maxwell we would find out what the bottom of the river is like; we would find out that it is not only possible, but practicable, to build these bridges, and to build them for an amount very much less than that estimated by Mr. Monsarrat, and put forward by the representatives of this Government -as the probable cost. I do not know any way of getting at this information, because, so far as I know, this Government has not paid any money in the matter. I suppose we might bring Mr. Maxwell before the Public Accounts Committee, but I d,o not want to go to that trouble. I am taking it for granted that this Government will bring down the papers and that we shall know exactly what kind of report Mr. Maxwell did make. They say that because of difficulties in crossing the river they are not going to take the line to St. John. They have eliminated the upper end at Grand Falls, making no connection with the Transcontinental; now they are going to eliminate the lower end,, and run the line down to a place called Welsford, or Westfield-they talk about Westfield, but I think they mean Welsford-and there they are going to tie on to the Canadian Pacific railway. This line, in respect of which the people of New Brunswick have guaranteed bonds to the extent of $6,000,000, starts in a beautiful little country town called Centreville, one of the finest places I know of on the continent of America, and stops at another beautiful little place called Westfield, a summer resort on the line of the Canadian Pacific railway.
And, Sir, that is the kind of road which the province of New Brunswick has got for its $6,000,000, and it is from the business

of that branch line proposition that we are going to receive the money with which to pay the interest on these bonds. Can you imagine a man from our province, no matter what his political affiliations may have been, who knows the conditions as we know them, discussing this thing without evincing a little heat, or at least a little concern for the future welfare of his province? If we were like some other provinces of Canada, it might not be such a serious matter. If we were like the great province of Ontario with its two and a half millions of people; if we had the enormous resources which they possess; if we had the enormous resources of even British Columbia, or of any other province, excepting Prince Edward Island, then we might not be so concerned. But I am sorry to say that our revenue producing resources are very limited. It is true that we have magnificent Crown lands. These are our principal source of revenue outside of direct taxation and of the subsidy which we receive from the Government here. But these Crown lands are being taxed to their utmost capacity, and have been for the last five or six years; that is, the Government are allowing the operatives to cut more timber from these lands than they should allow, with the Tesult .that they are becoming depleted to such an extent that, if things go on as they have been doing for the next twenty-five or thirty years, our Crown lands will not produce one-half of the revenue which they are producing at the present time. We have reached the absolute limit of our revenue which can properly be derived from the production of our Crown lands; we have a small amount of coal mining, but it is not very great and yields very little revenue; and, so far as I know, there are no other resources in the province of New Brunswick, outside of the subsidies which we receive from the Dominion Government, except direct taxation. Our population, I am sorry to say, has not increased very rapidly. I think it has only increased to the extent of about 20,000 in the last ten years, and I do not see any great prospects of any very rapid increase in the near future.
Under conditions like these, I do not think any man in the province could sit still when he considers that $6,000,000 have been added to the debt of the province in order to produce a railroad such as I have described. In making this statement I am not finding fault with the railroad itself.

It is true that portions of it, north of Fredericton, are pretty hilly and crooked, but it is well ballasted; it is pretty well drained; it has 80-pound steel rails; the ties are all right, and it runs through a beautiful, fertile, and productive country. But it is only agricultural country, and you require an enormous amount of agricultural products in the vicinity of a road like this, to produce business, forty per cent of the value of which will go to pay the interest on $6,000,000.
If we are to believe what we read in the newspapers of New Brunswick, it would seem that there is another scheme on foot. I hope my hon. friend the Minister of Public Works, who, I assume, is going to answer for the Government, will be able to answer this question definitely and positively. It is announced, and it is beyond peradventure, that the railway will not go farther north than Centreville, and not farther south than Westfield, serving an agricultural country terminating at one end at the village of Centreville, fifty miles south of the Transcontinental railway, and at the other at the Canadian Pacific railway, and making connection with it at two points. They say that if they get the money from the Prudential Trust Company, the proceeds of the .sale of those bonds will build the railroad to Westfield. When completed, the liability of the province >vill be in the vicinity of $6,000,000. Of course, in addition to that, this Government has paid a double subsidy on the whole 170 miles, but the Dominion treasury is rich compared with that of New Brunswick, and we are not finding so much fault with that part of it.
In addition to the plan I have outlined, they also state that they are going to build a road from a point seven or eight miles above Fredericton, to the American boundary line at a place known as Vanceboro. I hope this is not true.
It is said that the engineers of this Government have actually been surveying.

I have heard of a few
wild-cat and unreasonable schemes in my lifetime in connection with railroads and governments,-none of us are perfect, and we do not profess to be-but when it comes to asking the province of New Brunswick to build another railroad from a point near Fredericton to the American boundary line at Vanceboro, which must be at least 40 miles distant-I do not see how you can

get from any point above Fredericton to Vanceboro without travelling a distance less than 40 .miles-to build a road like that, well, I think we shall have reached the limit of endurance, and the Government shall have reached the limit almost of political impudence. The Canadian Pacific railway has a line from Fredericton to the International boundary line, and a splendid road it is. They give the people all the service which the people could ask for in that vicinity. If you want to go from Fredericton to St. John or to Boston, or to St. John or Woodstock or Edmunds-ton, or to any of the points in the western portion of New Brunswick, you have all the accommodation on the Canadian Pacific railway, which any person could reasonably ask, in conjunction, of course, with the present Valley railway which goes up the St. John river. If you wish to bring a carload of freight from Nova Scotia or from the eastern portion of New Brunswick to Fredericton, you might possibly use the Intercolonial railway, which they do not use at the present time to any very great extent, but they would be compelled to hand the freight over to the Canadian Pacific railway, which would transport it about 67 miles to Vanceboro where they join the Maine Central or American system of railways. I have indicated that the distance from Fredericton to Vanceboro by the new road would be somewhere about 59 miles, 10 miles by the present Valley railway, and the remaining 40 miles by the newly constructed road. I admit that 40 miles is only an estimate, but I know the location pretty well, and I think I am about right in my estimate. I have talked this matter over with the Intercolonial men, and I know that that is their intention. Suppose that you want to bring lumber or fish from northern New Brunswick, or anything which is produced in Nova Scotia for the American market, to Fredericton; of course they can bring it, if we want to make them bring it, over the Canada Eastern portion of the Intercolonial to Fredericton. In other words Fredericton could be made a central point for Intercolonial business going to the United States, but I do not think it would ever pay. I think it would be cheaper and more economical to bring it to St. John, and hand it over to the Canadian Pacific railway. But the Canadian Pacific railway would get the 90 mile haul of that freight, whereas if they brought it to Fredericton,! the Canadian Pacific railway would get only the 67 mile haul. Let us see how that works out. You
have only to make a simple computation. I think I can give it to show the utter nonsense of the whole proposition. If you are catering for the trade of the northern part of the province of New Brunswick there is not much traffic outside of lumber and some fish. Bo not forget that within the last two years this Government has bought 112 miles of railway running from Campbellton, in the northern part of New Brunswick, across the province and striking the American system of railways at St. Leonard's and Van Buren in the state of Maine. The Intercolonial railway is now connected with the American system of railways, from the northern part of New Brunswick, which would take in Bathurst, Dal-housie, Campbellton, and all the northern lumber region. The distance from Bathurst to the American system of railways, at Van Buren would be less than the distance from Bathurst to the American system of railways at Vanceboro. But, of course, the freight rate would be a little greater from Van Buren to Boston than from Vanceboro to Boston. From the Miramichi region, which is the greatest lumber producing portion of that part of New Brunswick, the freight rate down to Boston would be some 18 or 19 cents per 100 pounds. I have not looked into it lately but I think I am within half a cent of the actual rate. It is about 550 miles, I suppose, from the Miramichi, or from Newcastle, to Boston, and Boston, I may tell the House, is the distributing point for all freight emanating from the Maritime Provinces for the American trade. That would give you one-tenth or one-eleventh of the freight rate on a mileage basis which would be less than two cents per 100 pounds. Assuming that it would be two cents per 100 pounds, the average weight of a car of lumber will be, say, 50,000 pounds because 12,000 feet of lumber at 4,000 pounds per thousand is the maximum and that would make 50,000 pounds per car. I may be away above it rather than under it because the great majority of the lumber is seasoned and it will not run more than 3,100 to 3,200 pounds per thousand feet. If you take it at 50,000 pounds, and at a two cent rate, you have only $10 for transporting that car of freight from Fredericton to the international boundary line at Vanceboro, and the province of New Brunswick would get 40 per cent, or $4.40, for transporting that car of freight. Talk of building a railway to give the Intercolonial connection between Fredericton and Vanceboro in order that it may be able to quote rates direct

from the point of shipment to the American railway system when all we get is $4.40 as our share for transporting a car load of freight. I assume that it will cost $1,500,000 to build that road from a point 10 miles above Fredericton to Vaneeboro, a distance of forty miles. We cannot at the present moment borrow money for less than 5J per cent. I doubt very much if we province of New Brunswick could get money at 51 per cent. It is true that we sold some local bonds during last September, October and November at 5 per cent, but it was not a very large amount, the bonds were exempt from taxation which made them fairly attractive for estates, and they were pretty nearly all taken up by people representing estates in the province -of New Brunswick. At the rate of 5J per cent the interest charge would be $75,000 and at $4.40 per car you would require 17,500 cars of goods in the year to pay the interest on the cost of that 40 miles of road. Seventeen thousand five hundred carloads of goods would more than average 56 a day for every working day in the year. Does anybody believe you could produce 58 carloads of freight in eastern New Brunswick every day in ^he year for the American market? You could not produce 8 carloads per day in eastern New Brunswick for the American market every day in the year. I do not think you could produce 20 carloads every day in the year if you took in the whole of the Maritime Provinces. There is no doubt that on some days you could do a very large business, but there would be weeks when you would have nothing to do at all. If these were all converted into lumber, and fortunately lumber goes into the United States without paying duty, it would take about 200,000,000 feet of lumber more than is produced to furnish the Intercolonial railway with sufficient traffic to pay our share of the interest on the enormous cost of building that 40 miles of railway.
Does the Dominion Government, or the Minister of Railways or the Intercolonial Railway, intend to drive the little province ,of New Brunswick into a trade like that? If they do, then I have less respect for the Government of New Brunswick even than I have for the Government of Canada to allow themselves to be be driven into a deal like that. The Government of New Brunswick had the solemn pledge of their political friends in Ottawa, and they had the solemn pledge of their political opponents at Ottawa, that the Parliament of
TMr. Carvell.]
Canada and the Government of Canada would operate this railway on a 40 per cent basis, would connect it with the Transcontinental railway at Grand Falls, would build these bridges and would put us in a position to earn sufficient money to pay the interest on the bonds. Any Government in New Brunswick that would allow themselves to be driven into a deal like that deserves the anathema-I would like to say-of this House of Parliament, but I will not say that because it would not be parliamentary; but it deserves-my hon. friend says annihilation. No, annihilation is not sufficient. Turning a Government like that out of power is no punishment whatever for the sins that they have committed or will commit if they allow this transaction to go on.
Now that I have stated the case as briefly as I could, I do hope that the minister will tell us exactly what sort of a trade they have forced upon New Brunswick, and what kind of trade the subservient Government of New Brunswick have agreed to in order to get them out of some of their difficulties. We are asked to add another $1,250,000 or $1,500,000 to our debt. What is our debt to-day? It is pretty hard to say what the debt of New Brunswick is, because it may surprise you when I say that the present Government of New Brunswick will not tell us what our debt is. The Opposition tried during a whole session of Parliament to find out what the debt was. I should not say the Opposition, but I should say that the member from Northumberland, Mr. Stewart, a gentleman who was elected to support the present Government, tried during the whole session of 1915 to find out what our debt was. Would you believe that the Government would not tell him? The people of New Brunswick do not know how many million dollars they owe. We do not know, but if you will take the Auditor General's report for the year ended October SI, 1914, you will see that there was a bonded debt of $8,175,000 or thereabouts. They claim, which I believe is true, that they have a sinking fund amounting to nearly half a million dollars, and we have a little over half a million dollars to our credit at Ottawa. But that still leaves $7,000,000 of a bonded debt. But we know that that does not really represent the actual debt of the province of New Brunswick. We know that they have been issuing bonds by the millions since October, 1914, and I have no hesitation in saying that the bonded debt of New Brunswick is $8,000,000 and probably $8,500,000. In addition to that, we have incurred a debt of about

$300,000 in connection with the railway in the county of Gloucester, which, I am sorry to say, has been closed down and has become a liability of the province. We have $155,000 of bonded debt which we have assumed in connection with the Southampton railway, the railway from which a member of the local legislature cleaned up $35,000 or $45,000 for himself without having returned one cent to the Government.
What has become of that money?

What has become of the money? Pinder has got the money yet. A Conservative lawyer in St. John was appointed some time ago to see Mr. Pinder and get that money back, but it is one of those friendly things that does not amount to very much and, no proceedings have yet been started. If they can get through this session of the legislature and this session of Parliament without the suit being started that will be the end of it. I understand that Mr. Pringle, the Royal Commissioner, found the amount to be $33,000 or $34,000. As a matter of fact, it was $50,000 that was swiped out of the construction of that road. But that is a small thing in New Brunswick. The Minister of Public Works (Mr. Rogers) is sometimes told that he is a sinner, but I sometimes think he is not to be compared with them. He ought to watch that crowd. As he was handling millions in Manitoba, the small percentage was not so bad, but when you consider what was taken out of the little amount of money that is handled in the province of New Brunswick you must admire the ability of the people down there along the line of taking what does not belong to them.
Where do you get the percentage in Manitoba?
I have not figured it out.
You had better not make any statement until you figure it out.
We know it approximately. .
My hon. friend was dealing directly with myself. If he is going to make insinuations, I should like him to back them up with a definite statement.

I was talking about the Government. I do not want to be unpleasant. I thought I was complimentary in drawing such a distinction between the Minister of Public Works and the party in
New Brunswick. That was my intention, anyway.
You were referring to me personally.

In addition to the two
railroads I have mentioned, we know that the Valley railroad will run up to about $6,000,000. When you add these together, I cannot see where one-tenth, or at all events one-fifth part of the interest on that debt will ever be earned by that road, under present conditions. You have there an indirect debt of $6,000,000 anyway, which brings the total debt of the province of New Brunswick up to something like $13,000,000.
$26,000,000 in Alberta.
That is bad enough, but it is not half so bad as New Brunswick with $13,000,000. My hon. friend knows both intimately.

I know there is
no comparison between the reckless extravagance that characterizes the Government of Alberta, and the decent administration of the New Brunswick Government.

I am not going to argue that point just now. I am trying to look after the Government of New Brunswick, and incidentally trying to keep this Government straight, as far as that is possible; but when the two get together it's a pretty bad combination. I have tried to point out the financial situation of New Brunswick, in a very hurried manner of course. ,1 have tried to state as accurately as I could the actual position of railway affairs in our province. I have pointed out what we in New Brunswick know: that the Government of New Brunswick, aided and abetted by this Government, have decided not to build this joad north of Centreville, and not to build the bridges that would allow of direct connection with St. John. They have decided to make connection with the Canadian Pacific railway either at Welsford or at Westfield. We are told-and it is currently stated all over the province of New Brunswick-that the local Government, at the instigation of this Government, I believe, are to spend another quarter of a million or half a million dollars in building a road from near Fredericton to the American boundary. That road is absolutely unnecessary. It has not even the virtue of gaining political support for the party, for it does not pass through a country that is inhabited; there are not votes along the



line of railway. There is no business for the road. It rnns very largely through that granite region through whioh the Canadian Pacific railway, from Vanceboro east towards Fredericton Junction, rune; not altogether, but very largely. There might be a little business available in small lumber, but only a very small amount. I do not think that the Government of New Brunswick, in view of their experience with railroads during the last two years, want to go on with this road. Therefore, I can come to no other conclusion than that the Government of New Brunswick have been driven by this Government to enter into the monstrous transaction simply to gratify the whim and wish of Mr. Gutelius, the manager of the Intercolonial railway, who wants to have connection with the American system of railways independently of the Canadian Pacific railway. I think those who have known my connection with railway affairs in New Brunswick will know that I hold no brief for the Candian Pacific railway. I have prophesied for the last five or six years that this road was only intended to be a branch line or feeder for the 'Canadian Pacific railway. On the other hand, I cannot see what earthly reason there is why the province of New Brunswick, in order to gratify the whim of Mr. Gutelius, should be compelled to rush into debt to the extent of $1,500,000 when the Canadian Pacific railway already have a road from. Fredericton to the international boundary; and it is as good a road as any they will build, and gives the people in that territory all the accommodation they could possibly require. From Fredericton to Boston there are two first-class passenger trains a day, and from McAdam Junction for all points south, and all points north as far as Woodstock, two trains a day. The Intercolonial railway could not give a better service than that; not ae good, I think. Why on earth the Intercolonial railway and the Government of Canada want to force the province of New Brunswick to go into this expenditure is something I cannot understand,. I have given the facts, and have given them truly, as I understand them. I am sorry the Minister of Railways and the Minister of Marine are not here, but they knew that this discussion was coming up to-day. At least the Minister of Railways did, for I told him, and I have no doubt whatever that the Minister of Marine an<^ Fisheries knew about it too. I" am sorry they are not here, but I hope that the 
Minister of Public Works or the other minister who follows me will give us certain definite information which I think we are entitled to have. In the first place, has it been decided that this road will not be built north of Centreville? Has it been decided that these bridges across the St. John and Kennebecasis rivers will not be built? Has it been decided to build the railway from its terminus at Gagetown over to Westfield or Welsford, and if so, which? Has it been decided that the Valley railway, so-called, shall not have an independent connection in the St. John valley farther south than Westfield? And, lastly, * has it been decided that the province of New Brunswick is to guarantee bonds in order to build a road from a point at or near Fredericton, or ten miles north of it, to a point on the American railway system near Vanceboro? If the minister will answer these questions frankly and fully he will be conferring a great favour upon the people of the province of New Brunswick, for not only his political friends, but his political opponents in that province are taking a very deep interest in this matter. No question in the public affairs of Canada is causing as much real thought in that province as is this question of the future of the Valley railway. Mr. Speaker, I have taken up much more time than I intended, and, the importance of the subject is my excuse for having dealt with the matter at such length.

speakeroldname: Hon. ROBERT ROGERS (Minister of Public Works):

Mr. Speaker, my hon. friend has been fairly mild in his discussion of this matter this afternoon, although at times he ihas given some slight evidence that he has been nursing his wrath to keep i$ warm in respect to the railway situation in the province of New Brunswick. I can quite understand my hon. friend, or any other hon. gentleman from the province of New Brunswick, having very serious complaints to make, both in this House and elsewhere, against railway legislation within the borders of that province. But what I wish to take objection to is that my hon. friend ventures to fasten upon the Minister of Railways or upon the Minister of Marine and Fisheries a responsibility for those conditions, the responsibility for which belongs to that side of the House and not to this. As my hon. friend has stated, the people of New Brunswick have had placed upon their shoulders the very heavy burden of something like $5,000,000, if his figures are correct.

I am not in a (position to know whether they are correct or not, but for whatever sum of money has been fastened upon the shoulders of the people of New Brunswick in connection with the construction of the St. John Valley railway, hon. gentlemen opposite are entirely responsible and blameable. The people of New Brunswick have a pride in natural development of their province and especially in the development of the national port in that province. A few years ago, when legislation was introduced in this Parliament for the building of a transcontinental railway to carry the trade of Canada to our great ocean ports, it was naturally to be expected that the location of the road would be such as to give not only the people of New Brunswick, but all the people of Canada the advantage of an outlet at their great national port of St. John. The reason why such a location was not determined upon is probably best known to hon. gentlemen opposite. All we know about the matter is what has been stated in this House and elsewhere. If I am correct in my recollection, the Minister of Finance in the previous Government, Mr. Fielding, dealt very fully with this matter, pointing out that the building of a transcontinental railway to the city of St. John would give that port a special advantage over other ports in the Maritime Provinces, and that therefore the line must be so located as to go to the centre of population in the Maritime Provinces, although he claimed that Moncton was not the centre, but that some point in Cumberland county would probably be the proper point. However, in adopting the course which was then adopted, the 'Government of that day were only following what has always been their policy-that of hanging up a railroad or anything else before the eyes of two or three or four contending parties and then endeavouring from a political point of view to play every end to the middle. That is what they were attempting to do in connection with the construction of the Transcontinental railway so far as the ports of the Maritime Provinces are concerned, and it is >as a result of that condition of affairs and of the misplaced location of the Transcontinental railway as determined upon at that time, that the people of New Brunswick, proud of their national port, and of the resources of their province, have assumed this great liability for the construction of the Valley railway which, unmi
doubtedly, was the line that should have been followed by the Transcontinental.

In that case, how
was it going to get to Nova Scotia?

It would get to Nova
Scotia just the same as it does to-day. You had the 'Intercolonial railway then, to to take your traffic to Nova S'cotia; you have the same to-day, and what was the good of building a transcontinental railway if it was not for the purpose of carrying the traffic of Western Canada to our great national ports in the Maritime Provinces. We, who are interested in this railway outside of the province of New Brunswick, look to St. John as our closest national winter port for the shipment of goods coming from Western Canada. Those are the circumstances which originally placed upon the shoulders of the people of New Brunswick the responsibility for the building of this Valley railway.
. My hon. friend has taken up a great deal of time in dealing with the local conditions and circumstances surrounding the construction of that railway. He has reflected to some extent upon the Government of the province in which he lives, and I am sorry he has so reflected on my hon. friend the Minister of Marine and Fisheries as to insinuate or imply that that hon. gentleman is not present here to-day because he wanted to be absent as this question was to be brought to the attention of the House by the hon. member for Carleton. Mr. Monsarratt replied as follows:
Dear Sir,-I have the honour to acknowledge your letter of February 26th, enclosing copy of report prepared by Mr. C. B. Brown, comparing two alternate routes of the St. John and Quebec railway between Gagetown and St.John, one known as the bridge route, which includes a bridge over the St. John'river near the Mistake, dealt with in my report of February 23rd, 1914, and the other known as the Westfield route, and requesting me to advise you as to the comparative economies in construction and operation of the two routes and a recommendation as to the route that should be followed.
