On receipt of that, Mr. Gutelius addressed the following letter to the acting Minister of Railways and Canals (Mr. Reid), on the same date, February 28:
Moncton, N.B., February 28, 1916.
Dear Mr. Reid,-In response to your request for information as to the status of the St. John and Quebec railways matters, I may say that the matter has been frequently discussed between Honourable Mr. Cochrane and myself with the view to working out an alteration of the arrangement in view of the changes which have taken place in conditions since the inception of the enterprise. I beg to advise that the original objects in the construction of this line were,
1st. To provide transportation facilities for the productive portions of the St. John Valley in that province; and
2nd. To secure an independent direct railway connection between St. John and the Transcontinental railway, which was to bo leased to the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company.
The first object has been largely attained in the construction of the line between Gagetown and Centreville, which has been in operation for more than a year.
The second object can be attained by the Transcontinental railway which is now being operated as a portion of the Canadian Government railways system, connection being made at McGivney's junction by the Canada Eastern with the St. John and Quebec railway at Fre-deriction and thence to St. John by such route as it may be decided to construct. Consideration of the extension of the St. John and Quebec railway from Centreville North may well, in view of the financial situation caused by the war be deferred until a more favourable period and in the meantime efforts should be directed to the rapid completion of direct connection with St. John and also to obtaining by means of other connections as much profitable through business as can be secured for the St. John and Quebec railway.
In the matter of the construction of the line from Gagetown to St. John, it was originally provided in the Acts and Agreements that the line should be constructed on the East side of the St. John river, and connected with the Intercolonial in the vicinity of Rothesay. The Dominion Government originally agreed to guarantee bonds for $1,000,000 towards the cost of construction of the bridges over the St. John and Kennebecasis rivers, and later agreed to construct bridges over these rivers if found feasible.
We have gone into the matter thoroughly, and find from the surveys and reports that the bridge over the St. John river alone would cost $2,163,000, which would require the construction of piers in such depth of water and soft material

that would make the success and cost of the construction problematical. Owing to the hazardous construction, the tremendous cost, the cost of maintenance, its interference with navigation on the St. John river, the annual fixed charge of $120,000, which would be made up of interest and maintenance and operation costs, and the length of time required for its construction, it was felt that in the public interest some other route if possible should be found; and after making study of the country between Gagetown and St. John, it is found that we can reach St. John Union depot by remaining on the west side of the St. John river via Westfield, by a route which if following the river, is at most one mile longer than the Bridge route above described, and that this railway can be constructed for $707,000 less cost to the St. John and Quebec railway for their portion and save the $2,163,000 cost of bridges to the Dominion Government, or a saving to both governments of $2,870,000 as compared with the Bridge route, and our engineers are of the opinion that the Westfield route could be shortened considerably when making their final location surveys. This route is not encumbered with the difficulties above recited in connection with the Bridge route, and, besides the large saving in original expenditures, it possesses no disadvantages, and has the advantage of three miles less distance from the Transcontinental to West St. John, which will always be a large factor in the export business at St. John, although Courtenay bay improvements are the ultimate objective for export business at St. John for Canadian Government railways.
In view of the above and the recommendation of Mr. C. B. Brown, Chief Engineer, Canadian Government railways, in his letter of February 26th, Mr. C. N. Monsarratt, Chairman and Chief Engineer Quebec Bridge Commission in his letter to me of February 28 th, and Mr. Brown's letter of February 28th, copies hereto attached, it is recommended that the New Brunswick Government be urged to take up and consider a route on the west side of the St. John river, and that a connection be made with the Canadian Pacific railway at a point at or near Westfield where the construction of the St. John and Quebec railway shall terminate. If this is acceptable then the Dominion Government will secure from thei Canadian Pacific railway running rights from the point of connection to St. John over the Canadian Pacific railway on some reasonable basis to be arranged, pending final decision as to the best manner of entering St. John by an independant line to reach the Union depot, the main yarrds and Courtenay bay.
To do this may make it necessary to construct a low grade and independent line from Westfield,, which could be done by constructing a bridge over the St. John River, making the entrance to the St. John Union depot on a viaduct over Mill street. This would involve the construction of a new train shed on the site of the burned elevator, together with a double track freight line for the business of the Canadian Government railways and the Canadian Pacific railway, which would ultimately be followed up by the construction of a new passenger station and passenger terminal facilities.
It is further proposed that in view of its proximity to the Maine Central railway, a connecting link be constructed between the St. John and Quebec railway and the Maine Central railway.
A connection of this character would give the city of St. John a second independent railway connection with New England; besides it provides a short line to New England points from the central and Northern portions of the province. It would become the Canadian Government railways main line for forest products business destined to New England points from the railways under our charge tributary thereto, and would enable us to secure a better division of through freight and passenger rates than we are able to secure at present by the more circuitous routes.
It is recommended, therefore, that authority for the construction of a branch line under the St. John and Quebec railway charter, be granted, to connect it with the Maine Central railway by the most feasible route.
Yours truly,
(Sgd) F. P. Gutelius.
Hon. Dr. Reid,
Acting Minister of Railways and Canals, Ottawa, Ont.
In view of this recommendation from the officers of the Transcontinental railway to the acting Minister of Railways and Canals, it became the duty of the acting Minister of Railways and Canals to submit the proposals contained in the letters, which I have just read, to the Government of the province of New Brunswick. This was done in a letter written on 1st March by the acting Minister of Railways and Canals, and addressed to the Prime Minister of that province:
Ottawa, 1st March, 1916.
Dear Mr. Clarke:
Some time ago you wrote Honourable Mr. Hazen and asked him to interview Honourable Mr. Cochrane, Minister of Railways and Canals, in reference to the St. John railway situation. Owing to Mr. Cochrane's present indisposition it has fallen to me, as Acting Minister during his absence, to go into this, and I sent for Mr. Gutelius and took the matter up with him. I have gone into it very fully and I must say that Mr. Gutelius is very strongly of the opinion that the feasibility of building the bridges across the Kennebecasis and St. John rivers is open to grave question and subject to such great-risk, and the cost together with maintenance for all time so great that it has convinced him and also me, that the route as originally proposed is not in the best interests of all concerned. In addition to that when your Government first went into this scheme it was with a view of affording a connection between the Grand Trunk Pacific and the city of St. John. Since that time the Government has been obliged to take over and operate the Transcontinental railway, and as the Intercolonial railway already has a first-class connection with the Transcontinental railway at McGivney's, this alters the entire situation, and I believe a reconsideration of the proposal and a re-arrangement of plans will result in much better business to the St. John and Quebec railway, and a much better service to the citizens of St. John and that portion of New Brunswick served by the St. John and Quebec railway.
After discussing the whole matter thoroughly with Mr. Gutelius I had him put in writing a suggested re-arrangement of the scheme. I also had him take up the question of bridges with his Chief Engineer as well as Mr. C. N. Mon-

sarrat. who is in charge of the construction of the Quebec bridge, and both are strongly of the opinion that Mr. Gutelius' proposition is the one that should be adopted.
I asked that you come here or send some one to represent your government to discuss this matter, and I was very sorry indeed to hear that you were ill but was very glad to meet Honourable Messrs. Murray and Baxter to-day. I have gone into the matter thoroughly with them, have explained it fully and am now enclosing you a full copy of the correspondence which has passed recently in connection with the proposal.
Before taking this matter up with the Premier and members of the Cabinet I thought it advisable to submit this to you and your government for their consideration and would ask that after having considered it you would advise me what conclusion is arrived at.
Of course, you can understand that if it is agreed that the proposed re-arrangement is acceptable to both parties then the proposed construction of the bridges across the Kenne-becasis and St. John rivers is abandoned, and that you will at once proceed with the new route and have it reach Westfield at the earliest possible date.
It does strike me that if this re-arrangement is carried out, and if the city of St. John by this means secures two routes through Maine to the New England States it is of very great Importance to the people of your province.
As soon as you are able to consider this matter and let me have your decision I will then submit the entire question to the Dominion Government, and if it is approved will be glad to submit to the House any legislation that may be necessary for the purpose of giving effect to the conclusions arrived at.
Tours very truly,
J. D. Reid,
Acting Minister.
The Honourable Geo. J. Clarke,
Prime Minister of New Brunswick, Fredericton, N.B.

It was suggested by my hon. friend that the Government are not keeping faith in the matter of the construction of these bridges for the purpose of carrying out this railway project as was promised by this Government under legislation adopted by this House. But, in view of the fact that it has been discovered that we can get connection with St. John and save the Dominion of Canada $2,163,000, the estimated cost of building a bridge over the St. John river at Mistake, and in view of the saving, as suggested by the report of the engineers which I have just read, to the

province of (New Brunswick, of $700,000, I think that the House and the country will agree that the officers of the Intercolonial railway and the Government of the province of New Brunswick are acting wisely and well in the public interest, especially under present conditions, in saving that amount of money, and also in view of the fact that they are going to get practically the same results in the end. That, to my mind, is the important condition. The Government are trying in no way to escape the responsibility for the undertaking which they assumed in connection with the construction of these bridges. The conditions since that time have entirely changed by reason of the fact that the Grand Trunk Pacific have failed to take over the Transcontinental railway and in view of the fact that we have the advantage to-day of a connection at McGivney junction with Fredericton and that with the construction of this railway from Gagetown to St. John, we will have direct connection with that great, national port through which our products will be shipped during the winter months.
My hon. friend this afternoon quoted at some length from a statement made by the Minister of Marine and Fisheries in 1912, in which the minister stated very definitely that the line would undoubtedly be built from Centreville to Grand Falls. The hon. member for Carleton also quoted from a speech by the Minister of Marine and Fisheries two years later, when the minister had some little doubts as to the carrying out of this proposal. I would point out that the Minister of Marine and Fisheries was absolutely right in making the statement he did in 1912. Any man knowing the conditions, and the purpose for which the Valley railway was constructed, namely, that of making connection with the Transcontinental, would have made the same statement as the minister made in 1912. At that time he did not know that the Grand Trunk Pacific were not going to take over- the Transcontinental, but when he made his statement in 1914 he probably had some intimation of that possibility, and of our having the connection we have to-day. In view of the fact that we have that connection, there is no pressing need at the moment for the construction of the line from Andover to Grand Falls. 'Though I am not in a position to know, I believe that the 'Government of New Brunswick are bound to carry out their proposition; they are anxious to do it, and I am satisfied that they will do it as soon as it is possible. In
the meantime, their first duty is to make connection between Gagetown and the city of St. John.
My hon. friend also dealt at some length with the terms of the agreements between the province of New Brunswick and the Railway Department. I should like now to place on Hansard a statement I have received from the department with respect to this matter. Much of the information contained in this statement has already been supplied to the hon. member in reply to questions he had placed on the Order Paper. The statement is as follows:
We commenced operations between Fredericton and Centreville on January 1st, 1915, on the understanding that the deficiency in receipts, if any, would be borne equally by the province and the Dominion. This arrangement was terminated on March 31st, 1915, with the Provincial Government owing us $2,977.51-their half of the deficit. On April 1st a service on a new basis was instituted whereby the Railway Company and the Provincial Government were to receive 40 per cent of the gross earnings, and we also on May 31st undertook the weekly operation of the portion constructed between Fredericton and Gagetown. The result of these operations was a deficit of $24,579.40, and in addition there is due the province and the Railway Company 40 per cent of the gross earnings, amounting to about $18,733.65. Thus the total deficit for the nine months, to December 31st, 1915, on account of this transaction amounted o $4?,313.05, to which should be added the net deficit to us for the first three months of 1915 of $2,977.51, making a total deficit for the year's operation of $46,290.56.
It was this result of the first year's operation that convinced the Minister of Railways that the operation of the road was bound to be a losing proposition unless it could be continued to St. John and also connected with an American road in order that the line could obtain the benefit of through business West and South.
Due notice was therefore given the Railway Company and the Provincial Government that the forty and sixty per cent arrangement would cease on December 31st. The department's action in this respect was based on a legal opinion of the Department of Justice, a copy of which will be brought down with the correspondence.
Since the first of the present year the Government railways have been operating and retaining the entire receipts, subject, of course, to an agreement which has yet to be reached between the Dominion and the province as to whether any portion of the receipts shall be turned over to the province before the completion' of the road and while the road is losing money.
The St. John and Quebec railway has not yet been paid any portion of the forty per cent that is due them, for the reason that during construction we supplied them with rails, train service, track signs, etc., and expended considerable money in constructing local freight facilities, and also assisted them in the construction of their main line westward from the Fredericton "Y". In connection with these items, we have a considerable contra account, but these accounts are in process of adjustment between the parties concerned.
Did the minister state that since the first day of January the province has not received any portion of the earnings of the road?
My hon. friend is not correct in that impression. They have not received anything up to date. It is a matter of adjustment between the Railway Department and the province.
Has the Federal Government or the Department of Railways and Canals refused to carry out the 40 and 60 per cent arrangement?

They have not actually refused, but my horn, friend will have observed, that the statement mentioned a deficit of $46,000 in one year. The Minister of Railways was anxious to have a re-adjustment, and to have the road constructed from Gagetown to St. John in order that deficits might be avoided in the future. That is the proposition which he has so strongly pressed, and which has been accepted by the Government of New Brunswick. In the meantime the 40 and 60 per cent arrangement remains to be adjusted between the Minister of Railways and the *Government of the province of New Brunswick.
And, the Government of New Brunswick agrees to that?

I have not heard that they have agreed to it. The St. John and Quebec railway has not yet been paid any portion of the 40 per cent that is due.

On December 21, 22, 23, 24, and, 25, during the Christmas rush, two trips were made over that ehd of the

line each day. Since then a tri-weekly service has been given on Tuesdays, Wednesdays, and Saturdays, and will continue. My hon. friend complained this afternoon of the possibility of connection being mad,e between the Valley railway and an American line. I have already submitted to the House a letter in which Mr. Gutelius speaks of the advantage such a connection would be. But there are other points that might be closer than that. Would, not a line from Meductio to the 'American system be-

Would my hon. friend allow me? The distance from Meductic to any point on the American 'system of railways would be about the same distance as from Fredericton to Vanceboro, possibly five miles less, but two-thirds of that would be through American territory, and we would be compelled to build a railway through the state of Maine. That idea is more visionary than the other. You had better stick to the other.

It is not visionary. I am only stating the circumstances as they are presented to me.
I do not know that there is much more that the hon. member has stated that requires any answer. I have covered the ground so far as I understand the situation. The Government of New Brunswick apparently has accepted the proposal as made, and I am sure that it is acting wisely and well in eo doing, because a

double purpose is served, namely, a connection is given with the city of St. John to the Intercolonial and the Transcontinental, and it is assured that the Valley railway will, from the day the line is completed, become a paying proposition to the province of New Brunswick, the Dominion Government, and every one who has any connection with it. It is evident that it is running through a very good portion of the province of New, Brunswick, and, with the administration that it is certain to receive at the hands of the railway department, I am satisfied that it will be a paying proposition and of great advantage to the province of New Brunswick as well as to the Dominion.
I was a little sorry that my hon. friend was so bitter in his reference to the Government of the province of New Brunswick. As far as I understand the circumstances, and their attitude, they have but one purpose, to serve, and that is, to act in the best interests of the people whom they represent, by giving them the best arrangement possible under existing conditions. It is true, as I stated at the outset, that they had placed upon them the responsibility of building this Valley railway as the result of the incompetence and mismanagement of hon. gentlemen opposite in earlier days. They are, however, doing the best that can be done, and they are doing it in a manner that, I believe, is satisfactory to the people of that province.
My hon. friend told us a long story to-day about an investigation he had held, and about the Prudential Trust and so on, endeavouring to imply that there was something wrong in connection with the administration of the Government of New Brunswick, and although he referred to the investigation which was held and which he himself conducted not very long ago in that province, he forgot to tell us that, after he had held that investigation, there was an election in his own constituency owing to ,the resignation of the Premier of New Brunswick, who had formerly represented it; that the record of the Valley railway was submitted to that intelligent constituency-I think my hon. friend will agree with me that it is an intelligent constituency-and that their verdict was to give to the Government candidate a handsome majority of something like 700 votes, one of the largest majorities that the Conservatives have had in that constituency so far as I am aware. That is an evidence that
that Government of the province of New Brunswick are close to the hearts of their people, and that their conduct and their efforts to secure an extension of a railway system so necessary for the development of their province and of the great port of St. John, are such as to merit the confidence and respect of the people of that province.
There is nothing that this Government can do to assist in the carrying out of that enterprise that we are not prepared to do. We are prepared to assist generously and liberally, if it is necessary, in the extension of the railway that is to be carried on later between Westfield and St. John, and if there is expense in connection with the bridges there we will come to' the relief of the people of New Brunswick, believing as we do that it is in the interest of the people of Canada to >secure the most direct connection with that national port, and believing as we do that the connection, at MeGivney Junction gives us as direct connection as would the connection between Grand Falls and iSt. John, But that is a matter for the province itself, and the Provincial Government are no doubt anxious to carry out that .scheme, and they will no doubt do so at the earliest possible opportunity.
I do not know that there is much more to add from the point of view of the Railway Department. I have endeavoured to fulfil the request of my hon. friend and have frankly given the circumstances and all the facts connected with the negotiations that .have taken place between the Railway Department and the Government of the province of New Brunswick.

Mr. PUGSLE-Y:	My hon. friend has

That is the proposition.

I do not wonder that
the Government of New Brunswick has not signified to this Government its acceptance of such a proposition. I do not hesitate to say that such a proposition would be resisted most strenuously by the vast majority of the people of New Brunswick, because they feel that they have already on their shoulders a sufficiently heavy burden in connection with the Valley railway without undertaking a further obligation of two. or three million dollars for the purpose of getting another, and to my mind, utterly useless connection with the New England system. As my hon. friend from Carleton so well put it, the connection between St. John and Fredericton, Woodstock and all other points up and down the St. John river by means of the Canadian Pacific railway is now very satisfactory and answers every reasonable purpose, and for Mr. Gutelius to seek to have the people of New Brunswick undertake this additional burden of something like two or three million dollars is altogether a most startling proposition. There is another noteworthy point in this matter, and that is the extraordinary haste with which the correspondence seems

to have been completed. Here is an undertaking which has involved the province of New Brunswick in a liability of nearly $6,000,000, an obligation entered upon by the people of New Brunswick upon a distinct and positive understanding with both political parties that have the control of the affairs of Canada for a number of years. That understanding was that the road should be built from St. John to a connection with the Transcontinental railway at Grand Falls; that the road was to be buil't to a high standard, so that it might be used as part of a transcontinental system in bringing the traffic of our western country to the port of St. John. It was upon that positive understanding that the people of New Brunswick agreed to accept the obligation; an obligation of almost staggering proportions for such a small population.
Where does the hon. gentleman find that agreement? '

It is in the statutes. Let me tell the hon. gentleman where it was first found. The Provincial Government, a Conservative Government, recognized the desirability set forth by myself and our supporters from New Brunswick when I was a member of the Liberal Government, and negotiated with us for Government aid towards the construction of a railway up and down the valley of the river St. John. I remember that I insisted most strenuously-and I was backed up by all our supporters from the province of New Brunswick-that the road should form a part of the Transcontinental system. In the Dominion Railway Subsidy Act, we repealed all previous subsidy provisions, and provided for one subsidy for the whole road from St. John to Grand Falls, a distance of about 220 miles. There was found the first agreement, and in that proposition the then Government of New Brunswick heartily concurred. But they felt that before they could be justified in engaging the credit of the people of New Brunswick for the guarantee of bonds to the very laTge amount of $25,000 a mile, they must ensure beyond all question that the road was to be constructed from St. John to Grand Falls, so as to form part, as I have said, of the Transcontinental system.
There was another proposition, and that was that the Government of Canada should operate the line, when constructed, as part of the Intercolonial, and, no matter what the net earnings might be, should pay over

to the railway company, as protection to the province of New Brunswick, 40 per cent of the gross earnings of the road. I remember that it required a good deal of argument with my colleagues to get them to agree to that proposition. It was said to me-and said with a good deal of truthfulness-that forty per cent was a large proportion for the Government of Canada to pay over to the province, that the net earnings might not amount to so much, and that the amount to be paid to the province should be based on the net earnings. But I pointed out to my associates in the Government, especially to my hon. friend (Mr. Graham), then Minister of Railways, and to my right hon. friend (Sir Wilfred Raurier) then leader of the Government, that unless . some liberal arrangement of this character were made, it would be impossible for the company, even with the provincial guarantee, to raise the necessary money to enable the road to he constructed-for it was recognised that a larger amount would be r-equired than the amount of the Government guarantee. After a good deal of argument, my right hon. friend, (Sir Wilfred Raurier) came to the opinion that, as the valley of the St. John river was one of the oldest settled districts in the province of New Brunswick, having been settled for upwards of a hundred years, and yet was still, in many parts, without railway facilities, and as the road was to run through a most beautiful and fertile section of the country, the people of Canada might well undertake the obligation to pay forty per cent of the gross earnings to the company which should construct the road, which forty per cent, of course, would go, in the first place, to meet the obligations of the province in the guarantee of the bonds. The Government finally agreed to that proposition, and, if I remember rightly, a Bill was introduced and passed. I think the Act was passed when the late Government was in power. And that formed the first contract. Then I find that in 1912 a contract was entered into between this Government and the railway company, and also the Government of New Brunswick, providing for assistance towards the bridges in connection with the construction of the line. There were embodied in the statutes the two contracts made by the late Government of Canada and this Government, in which there was a positive and binding agreement upon the Parliament of Canada that a subsidy should be given for the railway all the way from St. John to Grand Falls, that,
as the road was completed in sections, the Government of Canada should take it over and run it, and pay to the province forty per cent of the earnings; and that the Government of Canada should aid in the construction of the bridges, and, later, that the Government of Canada should build the bridges with Dominion money. My hon. friend (Mr. Rogers), I think, cannot desire stronger evidence of that being the agreement as between the people of New Brunswick and the people of Canada acting through their Parliament. Yet, notwithstanding that solemn agreement, an agreement upon which the people of New Brunswick undertook these obligations-for it is not Premier Clarke, nor Attorney General Baxter, nor the members of the Provincial Government^alone who are committed to these obligations, they are to pay their share as taxpayers, of course; but it is the small population of 350,000 people in New Brunswick upon whose shoulders this enormous, this staggering obligation falls-the Minister [DOT]>f Public Works comes down and lightly tells this Parliament and the people of Canada that this solemn agreement is now to be set aside, and that this road, instead of forming part of the Transcontinental system, is to be merely a branch line of the Canadian Pacific railway-for that is all that it is to be. And in what time, do you think, were all these matters brought to a head? Mr. Brown writes a letter on February 26 of this year to Mr. Monsarratt in which Air. Monsarratt is asked to give his opinion with regard to the most desirable route to take. Mr. Monsarratt writes his answer on February 28, two days after the date of Mr. Brown's letter. Mr. Monsarratt's letter apparently reaches Mr. Gutelius on the same day, and on that day Mr. Gutelius writes to Dr. Reid, the acting Minister of Railways, acquainting him with the conclusion at which his engineers have arrived. This is the way this matter, the most important from a financial and business standpoint with which the people of New Brunswick have ever been called upon to deal, was considered. You find it considered by Mr. Brown's letter of February 26. You find Mr. Monsarratt has it before him and writes on February 28. On the same day Mr. Gutelius writes to Dr. Reid and on March 1, Dr. Reid writes to the acting Prime Minister of New Brunswick, suggesting that these changes have been recommended and asking what the provincial government think about it. Without taking the people of New Brunswick into his confidence, without waiting for the

meeting of the legislature in order to see what the representatives of the people thought about it, the acting Prime Minister wired Dr. Reid on March 7, approving of the proposed agreement, and followed it by a letter under the same date entirely agreeing with this proposition, which was of such enormous importance and which had its inception in Mr. Brown's letter of February 26, just a few days before. Do you think, Mr. Speaker, that that tells the whole story? Does my hon. friend the Minister of Public Works want this Parliament to believe that this matter had not been thought of and talked about and planned before this correspondence began? Why, Sir, the hon. member for Carleton has told you that there was ground for the suspicions of the people regarding the bona fides of the intentions of the Government of New Brunswick to extend the road to Grand Falls. If all reports are to be believed, the Canadian Pacific Railway Company gave their hearty support to the provincial government in 1912. It is well known that while Mr. Fleming, the then premier, was telling the people of Victoria county, from the public platform, that the road would run to Grand Falls as sure as the sun should rise the next morning, a prominent official of the Canadian Pacific Railway Company was stating that he had the positive pledge of Mr. Fleming that the road would never be built to Grand Falls. And, Sir, the suspicions of the people of that day are being verified by what is before us to-night. The first step toward fulfilling the pledge of the provincial government to the Canadian Pacific Railway Company, in violation of the solemn pledge they were making to the people of Victoria county and the people of St. John, was to do away, as the Minister of Railways got this Parliament to do away, with that portion of the subsidy -which was to apply to the railway between Andover and Grand Falls. That was the first step in this outrageous proposition which has been carried on, not openly, but consistently, from that day to this, in order to fulfil the pledge which Mr. Fleming made to the Canadian Pacific Railway Company; in order to carry out the plot which to-night is being consummated by the declaration of the Minister of Public Works that the St. John Valley railway is to begin at Centreville and is to end, so far as the undertaking of the Provincial Government is concerned, at Westfield,. Does my hon. friend question what I say? Let him take the letter of Mr. Gutelius. Perhaps it has 
not impressed itself on his mind; it did impress itself on my mind. Mr. Gutelius says, as clearly as words can state it, that the undertaking of the Provincial Government is to end at Westfield. In other worc^s, so far as the Provincial Government is concerned, this road is to be a branch of the Canadian Pacific railway, beginning at Westfield, running to Fredericton, and extending to Centreville, a small village about twenty-five miles north of Woodstock-in every respect a branch line of the Canadian Pacific railway. And, so the obligation to the Canadian Pacific Railway Company is being paid to-day. So are being fulfilled their hopes and their aspirations that the Valley railway, instead of being a competing line, instead of being part of a great transcontinental system, is to be simply a branch, an annex, an adjunct, of the great Canadian Pacific railway.
