Now, in view of the present proposition to have the project, so far as the St, John and Quebec railway is concerned, terminate at Westfield, I think that, before the whole scheme is broken up, this Government ought to be able to state to the House whether they are prepared to proceed with surveys and investigations, and within a reasonable time, to construct, as a Government work, the railway from Westfield into the' union station in St. John and to the yards at Courtenay bay.
But I object to this change for another reason. All the vast improvements .which weTe outlined and contracted for at Cout-tenay bay were a part of the undertaking to build a road from Grand Falls to Si. John, and to make it part of the Transcontinental Railway system. When the late Mr. Hays was president of the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company, he had many interviews with the Government. He considered very carefully the lay-out of the terminals at Courtenay bay, and his company, through the Grand Trunk Pacific Development Company, acquired a large area of land at the head of Courtenay bay. He looked forward with the greatest possible hope and confidence to the very near future when over the Valley railway there would come a vast transcontinental traffic, which would have its terminus at Courtenay bay. There were to be great yards there; there was to be an elevator, and there were to be the usual facilities which are always to be found in connection with great ocean terminals.
It was felt that it would be an infinitely better way to reach the terminals as it would be very much more convenient to operate railway trains than it would be if they came in from the western side. If they came from the western side it would be necesary to cross over from the west to the eastern side of the harbour of St. John in order to get to the docks at Courtenay bay and it would be necessary to have a system of switchbacks which would be inconvenient and add to the expense and delay of operating the terminal system. That is why Mr. Hays pronounced himself

absolutely in favour of what Mr. Mon-sarratt and Mr. Gutelius call the bridge route but which we speak of as the route coming down the eastern side of the river St. John from Mistake. My hon. friend cannot be unaware of the fact that these officials of the Grand 'Trunk Pacific the moment it was proposed to change the route and come down the western side of the river, publicly and emphatically declared their opposition to the change of route and said it was utterly absurd to do so it was expected that the road was to form part of The Transcontinental railway system.
But my hon. friend makes the excuse for all this change by saying that the Grand Trunk Pacific have failed to enter into, or carry out, the obligation to operate the Transcontinental railway. I desire to say, in the presence of the minister, that so far as this Parliament is aware, the Grand Trunk has never failed in its obligation to operate the Transcontinental railway. This Parliament has never had placed before it any information from which such a conclusion could be drawn. We do know that this Government, ever since it came into office, has consistently, persistently and deliberately altered the grades and made changes in the terminals of the Grand Trunk Pacific railway which gave the Grand Trunk Pacific an excuse for refusing to operate the road until the specifications were lived up to. That is all the knowledge this Parliament has in regard to the Grand Trunk failing to operate the Transcontinental railway. I would expect that before my hon. friend would make that statement he would give the information to the House upon which he bases it and show that the Grand Trunk Pacific has failed or refused to carry out its obligations.
I, Sir, with all respect to my hon. friend, do not believe one single word of it. My hon. friend may have misinterpreted

no doubt he has misinterpreted-what they have done, but I think it will be found upon examination of the correspondence that all they have done has been to insist upon the specifications of the road being carried out and lived up to by the Government, and I have no doubt that if that is done they will be prepared to enter into the lease which is provided for by the agreement, and which they cannot be expected to do otherwise.
I am extremely sorry that it has come to this. } I had hoped that our expectations that St. John would become the great port
in connection with the Transcontinental railway would have been realized. The people of St. John have long hoped that this would be the case, but when they read in the newspapers to-morrow morning the statement that my hon. friend the Minister of Public Works has made, they will feel that their hopes are blasted, and a feeling of disappointment will spread not only among the people of St. John but among the people of New Brunswick, who take pride in our great commercial city, and who looked forward to a day in the not very far distant future when St. John would be able to take her place as one of the great Atlantic seaports, and through which a vast deal of transcontinental business would be carried both in winter and in summer.
My hon. friend has talked about the cost of these bridges. I think from the correspondence that M,r. Gutelius had made up his mind that the eastern route shall be abandoned. I learned a year ago that Mr. Gutelius had made up his mind to that. How long ago is it that the Minister of Railways said that Mr. Gutelius had been loaned to this Government by the Canadian Pacific? Three years, was it? During that time Mr. Gutelius has done good work for those who loaned him to this Government, and to whose employ he will go back when his three years are up. He has Succeeded in placing St. John as a way station so far as the operation of the Intercolonial railway is concerned. He has arranged it so that any one desiring to go to Montreal will find it intensely inconvenient to go to Moncton to take the Ocean Limited, the best railway train which travels between the Maritime Provinces and Montreal. He will have to stay three or four hours in Moncton, and therefore he will find it infinitely better for his comfort, even if the route is not of as much scenic beauty, to take the Canadian Pacific line rather than attempt to catch the Ocean Limited. In all other respects it will be found that Mr. Gutelius has had an eye-a very open eye-towards Canadian Pacific interests.
May I ask my hon. friend, in all his busy life how many times he has travelled to Montreal from St. John by the Intercolonial railway?

I could not tell my hon. friend how many times I have gone to Montreal by either route during my bus) life, and, therefore, he is putting to me a hard proposition, but let me tell him that when Mr. Blair was Minister, of Railways, and wfien he placed St. John on the main



line, many of us used to take pleasure in travelling by the Intercolonial to Montreal. While the 'distance "is longer, the pleasure of travelling by the north shore of the province is greater.
In the winter?
No, the Ocean Limited, only runs in summer.
It runs in winter too.

Perhaps it does, but I do not think it is running now. But, in the summer there was no lovelier trip that one could take than from St. John to Montreal over the Intercolonial railway. The scenery of the Baie des Cl^aleurs and the Metapedia valley is simply gorgeous. But since this Government came into power it is only with the greatest possible inconvenience that you can go to Montreal via the Intercolonial railway because it involves spending three or four hours at Moncton.	.
Is the Mr. Blair to whom my hon. friend refers the same Mr. Blair who resigned because of the same Transcontinental railway to which reference has been made?

The very same gentleman, and it is wonderful, Sir, how many political crimes these gentlemen think they can justify by saying that Mr. Blair opposed something that the Liberal Government proposed to do some years ago. They must think that the people of this country can be humbugged.
They could until 1911.

If hon. gentlemen opposite think that they can make the people forget accusations of political mismanagement, crimes, and offences by saying that Mr. Blair had a difference of opinion with his colleagues several years ago as to the ' question of the route of the Transcontinental railway they are greatly mistaken. My hon. friend can take comfort from the fact, as I have no doubt that the Canadian Pacific will, that at last Mr. Gutelius has succeeded in so presenting the matter to this Government that they have agreed to abandon the St. John Valley railway as part of the Transcontinental railway and simply to run it as a branch line of the Canadian Pacific. But my hon. friend says that they will have running rights over the Canadian Pacific from Westfield, whereas, if the railway came over the eastern

route, crossing the Kennebecasis at Rothesay, it would run for nine miles over the Intercolonial railway. My hon. friend has forgotten that when they run over the Intercolonial railway they are running over the people's railway, and that the earnings, whatever they are, for that nine miles go into the treasury of Canada. When they run oyer the Canadian Pacific railway the earnings go into the capacious pockets of' the Canadian Pacific Railway Company. That is the difference. In one case it is the people's railway that would be benefited, and that would control the matter, so far as the terms are concerned; in the other case the business would be controlled by a private company, and the benefits accruing from the haulage over that mileage would go into the treasury of a private company, and not into the pockets of the people of Canada. Just a word in regard to the bridges, and I shall not detain the House longer.
Hear, hear.

I am glad to see that my hon. friend from Halton (Mr. Henderson) has a vigour that will enable him to bear the duties of a Privy Councillor for many years to come, I trust. I can assure him that I do not object to his crying " Hear, hear. " It shows he is awake,-
-Mr. R. B. BENNETT: Which you did not expect.

-which has not always been the case in the past. With regard to bridges, when this Government in 1912, and again in 1914, led the people of New Brunswick to believe that they were going to give this generous encouragement to the building of bridges, it was known then, just as well as it is known to-day, that those bridges would be expensive. The examinations which have been made since have not shown that the bridges would be more expensive than it was thought they would be. I know that Mr. Maxwell, who is the Chief Engineer of the Valley railway, and who was appointed by the Provincial Government, has made a further examination at the instance of the Provincial Government, and has reported that he found good foundations at reasonable depths. I am satisfied that his report will show that the cost of these. bridges, both the one across the St. John river and the one across the Kennebecasis, will not at all exceed what it was estimated they would cost when this Government entered upon the obligation to

build these bridges, and so aid the Provincial Government to that extent. In 1912 this Government promised aid in building the bridges in order to induce the people of New Brunswick to believe that they were disposed to act generously towards that province, which had assumed these great obligations. The legislation was passed by this Government about the time a provincial election was coming on. It would be grossly unfair for me to insinuate that the provincial election had anything to do with it. I know that my hon. friend who has knowledge of elections-that elections are to be won in only one way-would not include legislative promises in the way he thinks elections can properly be run. Therefore, to use the phrase of the Minister of Finance, I can only say that these two events synchronized in a most remarkable manner.

I should like to know
what is implied in the insinuation that my hon. friend directs to me.

I will tell my hon.
friend. My hon. friend has stated in this House that hon. gentlemen on the other side will realize that he knows how to run elections. That is all.

I have heard that statement repeated very, very often, but I have not taken any notice of it before because I am very good natured. The statement my hon. friend refers to I made in this House when I was dealing with the attitude of hon. gentlemen opposite in respect to the navy question, which was under discussion at the time. I said that I was prepared to submit to the people the record as presented by hon. gentlemen opposite on the floor of this House;'that I knew and understood what affected the people of Canada in respect to the winning of elections, and therefore knew that that question would carry.
I am very glad indeed to have my hon. friend throw around his statement the embellishment which he has to-night.
No embellishment. If you read Hansard you will see it.

My hon. friend has put it in a more ornate form, in which it does not seem so harsh as it did to those of us who heard him make it some two or three years ago. I apologize to my hon. friend if, for a single moment, I drew from the statement which he made the idea that he had reference to those less beautiful and more
122*
reprehensible means of winning an election which are sometimes resorted to. I cheerfully accept his statement, and feel that when anybody in the future intimates that my hon. friend knows how to run elections he has in his mind simply those broad and statesmanlike measures relating to the public good, in which the people would be likely to be interested, and which would therefore be likely to influence them in any decision at which they might arrive when they come to cast their ballots. I can assure my hon. friend that his words to-night ought to lift him to a higher plane and gain for him greater respect and esteem among the people of this country. At all events, these two events synchronized in a most remarkable degree.
This generous legislation made by this Parliament was passed just when a provincial election was impending in the province of New Brunswick. This Parliament, at the instance of the Government, authorized the granting of most liberal aid towards the building of those bridges. Well,' nothing has occurred to make it less reasonable to build those bridges to-day than when the legislation was passed. Afterwards, in 1914, the Government asked this Parliament to agree to the absolute building of three of the bridges. As has been well pointed out by my hon. friend from Carleton this afternoon, the people of New Brunswick took the word of this Government-I will not say for what it is worth, but for what the word of honourable statesmen ought to be worth. They took the word of this Government, and then entered upon increased obligations to the extent of $10,000 per mile additional. Believing that the road would be built from Grand Falls to St. John, they took these vast additional burdens upon their shoulders. And to-night they are Confronted with the statement that the obligations on the part of this Government are to be ignored. They will read the most remarkable statement read to this House tonight, in wkich the acting Minister of Railways, although this Government had entered into a solemn agreement to pay to the province 40 per cent of the gross earnings, notifies the Government of New Brunswick that that arrangement will have to be modified, that this Government is not prepared to carry out its obligation to pay to the province 40 per cent of the gross earnings, and that the province of New Brunswick must be prepared to bear its share of the losses that might occur from time to time. The
mo

people of New Brunswick are confronted with that absolute repudiation on the part of this Government. To-night, they find that further pressure has been brought to bear. A communication is sent to them asking them to agree to change the whole terms of the obligation which was entered into, and to abandon the idea of a Transcontinental line, and to consent to the building of a line which, as I have said, will simply be a branch line and an adjunct of the Canadian Pacific railway.
I wish simply to say, in conclusion, that I .for one, as representing the constituency of the city of St. John, am profoundly grieved to think that the Government is proposing to do an act of such gross injustice to the people of New Brunswick as is now proposed by the course of events which has been outlined by the Minister of Public Works to-night. Let me express the hope that the Government will consider the matter further. Let me express the hope that some time, at all events, will be given to the people of New Brunswick to make their views heard with respect to this matter. They should not be rushed into the transaction. I know how intense is the feeling of the people of St. John against modifying the original contract. I know how desirous they are of seeing that original contract carried out. And if I can hope to attain nothing else, let me express the earnest desire that the Government will pause before they enter into a binding obligation in this respect, and that they will at all events give an opportunity to the people of St. John and of New Brunswick to express their feelings in this matter. And I believe, if the Government will give heed to what is thought, not only by the people of St. John, but by all the people of New Brunswick, they will not act upon the lines which have been laid down by my hon. friend tonight as indicating what this Government has determined upon and what has been agreed to with the Government of New Brunswick.

As a representative of the county of Victoria, I am very much interested in this debate. The terminus of this Valley railway was to be at Grand Falls, one of the nice little towns lying along the St. John river, a progressive town with a large population and a fine surrounding district. A few years ago I followed, with great interest, the debate on this subject and I listened with great attention to the Minister of Railways when he said to my hon. friend from Carleton in

connection with the construction of this railway "Have faith." Well, faith will never build railways in New Brunswick. Faith would never have put the Flemming Government back into power in 1912, a railway had to be built in order to put that Government back into power. I followed also in that same debate the remarks of my hon. friend the Minister of Marine and Fisheries who, on that occasion, stated that he was just as sure as he was standing in the Chamber that the Valley railway would be built up to Grand Falls. That statement was made four years ago. I could quote his words from Hansard, but my hon. friend from Carleton has already mentioned the volume and the page at which his remarks are to be found. The Minister of Marine and Fisheries certainly had a vision that day, because the railway has never yet been built up to Grand Falls, and from what I know of the hon. minister, I am positive that that road will never be built up to that point as long as he has anything to do with the construction of it.	[DOT]
I have listened to-day to the remarks of my hon. friend the Minister of Public Works, and I believe he has the same vision as the Minister of Marine and Fisheries had. He seems to have a positive assurance that the railway will be built up to Grand Falls. Four years hence, if my hon. friend is on this side of the House, I will tell him that he has had his vision just as the Minister of Marine and Fisheries had. Now, it is just as important to-day to build this railroad as far as Grand Falls as it is to build it to St. John, because we want to have a through route from! the upper part of the province of New Brunswick down to the best winter harbour in the Maritime Provinces. I am not surprised that this railroad is not built as far as Grand Falls. In 1912, our friends the Tories won an election in my county on the question of that railroad. The two *candidates for the present administration stated to the electors of that county that, if they refused to vote for them, they would never have that railroad built as far as Grand Falls. The result was that a little Liberal majority turned into a small Tory majority and the Government elected their two candidates. Another election is coming on pretty soon, probably this year, in the province of New Brunswick, and in the copnt.y of Victoria something must be said in connection with this railway, and the people will probably again be called upon to give their vote to the Government

in order to have a terminus of the Valley railway at Grand Falls.
We have had a discussion on the question of a bridge to be 'built at Andover, and 1 understand from the reports given to-day that the bed of the river is not very good. There are to-day at Andover two bridges built across the St. John river, a highway bridge and a railway bridge, and I have never heard from any one yet that the bottom of that river is not suitable to support piers for a good railway bridge. We have many railway connections to-day between the province of New Brunswick and the state of Maine; we have connections between St. Leonards and Van. Buren, at Aroostook Junction, at Debec Junction, and at Vanceboro. I believe we have now enough railways from the province of New Brunswick into the .state of Maine. To-day we want to build railroads not going too much into the state of Maine; we want, if possible, railroads from the state of Maine into the province of New Brunswick. As far as the cost of building this road to Grand Falls and St. John is concerned, we have been called upon to pay interest on $4,000,000, and the work is not yet completed. It seems as if the present Government will have a deficit as long as that road is unfinished, and it is important that it should be completed from Grand Falls to St. John in order to give a long haul and thus ensure a good revenue to this Government and to the Government of the province of New Brunswick in order to operate the road in the best manner possible.

Mr. Speaker, I would not be doing justice to myself as a representative of the province of New Brunswick if I failed to add a word or two to the subject which is now under discussion and in which every citizen of New Brunswick must be very much interested. During the greater part of the time that this subject was under discussion in the Provincial Legislature, I happened to be a member of that body and therefore I know something about what took place-in regard to bringing down the legislation that finally resulted in the commencement of what is known as the St. John Valley railway. I remember back as far as 1904 and 1905 when this matter was brought up in the House of Assembly in the province and was discussed pro and con by the Government of the day and the Opposition which, at that time, was led by my hon. friend the Minister of Marine and
Fisheries. Delegations from different sections of that part of the province waited upon the Government, pressing upon them the great necessity of giving railway communication to that portion of New Brunswick. My hon. friend from the city of St. John, who, at that time, was a member of the Provincial Government, will remember that the whole discussion rested upon the only real proposition that could be considered : that of linking the railway up with some transcontinental system that would give direct entrance into the city of St. John. My hon. friend the Minister of Marine and Fisheries, who was the leader of the Opposition at that time, made in the Legislature of 1907 a speech in which lie used these words:
I am quite satisfied that as a purely local road the railway would not pay, and I have every confidence that as part of the Transcontinental system it would be highly beneficial to the province and would not cost the people anything at all.
These are the words of the-Minister of Marine and Fisheries, at that time leader of the Opposition in the province of New Brunswick. Shortly after he uttered these words he came into power as Premier of that province. I was a member of the provincial legislature at that time. As soon as the Government of the hon. gentleman (Mr. Hazen) came into office they took up the question of making some arrangement for building the railway down the valley of St. John. My hon. friend from the city of St. John (Mr. Pugsley) was a member of the Dominion Government of that day, and my hon. friend from Carleton (Mr. Carvell) was also a member of this House, and both of them took great interest in assisting the Provincial Government to arrange some reasonable sdheme by which the railway might be built. The proposition put forward was that the province of New Brunswick was to guarantee the bonds of the road from Grand Falls to the city of St. John at the rate of 125,000 a mile, and that when the road was completed the Intercolonial should take it over and operate it and pay 40 per cent of the gross receipts to the company. I know how long and thoroughly this matter was discussed and how anxious every member of the legislature was to give all assistance, so that this old-settled portion of the province, which was without railway accommodation while other portions of the province were well supplied, should be traversed by a well-constructed railway. They realized

Transcontinental to the winter port of St. John. What possible excuse can the Government give for taking their present attitude? My hon. friend says that it is going to be cheaper to build the road from Gage-town over to Westfield and on to St. John, than it would to build it the other way.
That is not the promise that was
10 p.m. made to the people of the province of New Brunswick. The promise made by the Government of New Brunswick, backed up and guaranteed by members of the Dominion Government, was that we should have a through line of railway from Grand'Falls to St. John. Now we are to have a short piece of road running from Centreville, in the county of Carleton, to Westfield, or, I believe, WeJsford, on the line of the Canadian Pacific railway. Upon the promise of the Government of the province of New Brunswick, and also of this Government, that they should have this through line, the province guaranteed the bonds and pledged their credit for at least $6,000,000. What have the province of New Brunswick got in return for the pledging of their credit and the spending of this money? Nothing but a short local line of railway from Centreville to Westfield-if they get it even to Westfield. I contend that the province of New Brunswick has not been fairly treated. With a population of only 350,000 people, they have been forced to pledge their credit to the extent of this large sum of money. It is a sin and a shame that this Government should attempt to assist the Government-of the province of New Brunswick to change their course, to continue their deception and their fooling of the people in this matter of railway accommodation, and to pledge their credit for so large an amount. It is putting a load on the shoulders of the [DOT]people of the province of New Brunswick that they are not able to bear. I sincerely hope that the Acting Minister of Railways and Canals, before giving the assistance proposed, will take up the matter earnestly and deliberately with the government of New Brunswick, and try to work out some arrangement by which the original intention, as regards this road, will be carried out, and so give to the people of that section of the province, a railway from Grand Falls to St. John along the route intended, on the east side of the river St. John. My hon. friend speaks of going across from Gagetown to Welsford.

I did not say Welsford.
(.Mr. Copp.]

I mean Westfield, but 1
venture to predict that my hon. friend will say Welsford before this time next year. As sure as the sun rises in the East and sets in the West, he will tell us that it will be from Gagetown to Welsford, on the Canadian Pacific railway. That is what will take place. My hon. friend will come here next year, and if he has the privilege of speaking as Acting Minister of Railways, he will say that things have changed, that Mr. Gutelius, Mr. Montsarratt, and Mr. Brown have told him that there is a better route up to Welsford. That is the excuse they are offering now in regard to the changed route, and they will offer it again next year. Ever since the hon. Premier of the province met Mr. Van Home at McAdam and rode in his private car to Montreal, as far back as that, it was decided that the Valley railway would be an adjunct of the Canadian Pacific railway, and nothing else. That was the belief then, and it has become stronger and stronger every day. My hon. friend this afternoon, when speaking of the route of the road, gave ample proof of the reasonableness of the doubt that has existed in the minds of the people of the province of New Brunswick. That doubt has not been dissipated, and in my opinion it never will be dissipated. Before many years have passed over the head of my hon. friend, he will find this road being operated practically by the Canadian Pacific railway, as part of their system, and the little province of New Brunswick will be obliged to pay interest on the bonds for all time.

Coming from the northern part of New Brunswick, from the country furthest from the district over which this railroad is to be built, I deem it my duty to say a few words. My hon. friend the Minister of Public Works has asked the people of the province to have faith in th^ Government. Faith is acquired or lost according to the direction given by the Administration. I believe it will take a great deal of persuasion on the part of the hon. Minister of Public Works to restore faith in the minds of the people of New Brunswick. This question of the St. John Valley Tailway is an old question in the province of New Brunswick. No local Government attempted io vote money for such a railway, because the other portions of the province, northern New Brunswick and eastern New Brunswick, were always opposed to it. The hon. Minister of Marine and Fisheries, when he was

leader of the Opposition in New Brunswick, declared that a road through that valley, operated as a local road, could neveT be made to pay its expenses. The people of northern New Brunswick, whom he represented in the Legislature, and whom we represent in this House, were never in a position to give a vote in favour of granting money towards the building of that railroad until it was proposed to make it a part of the Transcontinental railway from Grand Falls to St. John in order to ensure further development of the trade from the West to the maritime port of St. John. It was to be no adjunct of the Canadian Pacific railway, but part of the Transcontinental railway, starting from the proper point at Grand Falls to St. John. But the moment that the promise of the Government at Ottawa and of the Government at Fredericton was not carried out, the people lost faith. The moment that construction was not begun at Grand Falls, which from a business standpoint was the proper starting point, the moment the Government delayed carrying out that part of the contract and Grand Falls was left out, the people of New Brunswick lost faith in the negotiations between this Government and the Government of New Brunswick. To-day the people of the province are called upon to pay an enormous expense in connection with that railway, and in a deceptive way. They were willing to undertake the burden of that expenditure for the further development of Canadian trade, connecting with the Transcontinental railway, but not for a local road to suit the convenience of the Canadian Pacific railway, as has been well said by the speakers who have preceded me. I only wish to express my own feelings and to voice the disappointment and loss of faith of the people of northern New Brunswick in the Conservative Government at Ottawa and the Conservative Government at Fredericton.

If no other hon. gentleman has anything to say, I wish very shortly to refer to the frank confession made by the Minister of Public Works this afternoon. I thank him for his sincerity in explaining to us the position as, I think, it exactly exists, or at least exactly as it was given to him. If we have accomplished nothing else by this discussion we have cleared the atmosphere, and the people of New Brunswick will now know, not the worst, perhaps, but something about the
terms and financial burdens that are staring them in the face, and that are likely to continue for generations to come. Just here I should like to say that, while, perhaps, I am a hard political fighter, I am glad that my hon. friend the Minister of Marine and Fisheries, a gentleman for whom I have the greatest regard, has been saved the humiliation of being present this afternoon and listening to the confession made by the Government through the lips of the Minister of Public Works. I think we can also extend our sympathies, to some extent, to the Minister of Railways, whose illness has saved him the humiliation of coming here and making the confession himself, instead of having it made through the Minister' of Public Works, who, of course, has no great personal interest in the matter. From all that has been said by hon. gentlemen this side of the House, I think the Minister of Public Works must have been convinced that a part of the solemn pledge, or contract, between this Government and the Government and people of New Brunswick was that this road should be built from Grand Falls to St. John, and become part of the through line over which transcontinental business would pass. We have the positive statement of the Government of Canada that, so far as they were concerned, they did not want the road to go north of Centreville.
I did not say that.

Let us see. I did not take down my hon. friend's exact words, but he read, a letter from Mr. Gutelius, in which it was stated that they saw no advantage in building the road north of Centreville. But he thinks he can smooth it over for his friends in the province of New Brunswick and he said that they hoped, at some time in the future to carry out the contract and continue the road to Grand Falls. I think I am correctly giving the statement made by my hon. friend. As faT as the present is concerned, and the future'too, that is the end of it; it goes to Centreville and stops there. No matter what the ambitions and wishes of the local government in New Brunswick may be, without the hearty co-operation and assistance of this Government, without an undertaking that they will take over and Operate this road, no government in New Brunswick ever could get the money, or would ever dare try to get the money, to carry on the work. From the time this Government takes the attitude that they

will not operate the road north of Centre-ville, that is the end of it and it will never be built.	,
Then the Minister of Public Works has also stated that they are satisfied with the connection through McGivney junction because he states that the great object, so far as the people of Canada is concerned, is to get direct connection with St. John. It makes one laugh to hear the hon. gentleman dilate upon the advantages of that great winter port, about the anxiety of this Government to develop it and how the people of the city of St. John are going to see the business pass through it. I felt I could almost discern tears in my hon. friend's voice when he discussed that question. But in so far as they are ' concerned, the hon. gentlemen opposite are satisfied to have this business go through McGivney junction. The hon. gentlemen dilated upon the importance of having this road finished at once in order that this great volume of business might go through the port of St. John and that the province might be saved from any further loss. He has no hesitation in making the prophecy that the moment this road is cqmpleted down to some point on the Canadian Pacific sufficient business will go over the road to make it possible that -40 per cent of the earnings will pay the interest on $6,000,000. Has my hon. friend considered what that means? Of course, I know he has not, because my hon. friend naturally could not know very much about it. I gave him very great credit for the intelligence with which he discussed the matter this afternoon, not knowing the particular location. But he must remember that there are 52 plus 25 miles which makes 87, or 88, miles of this road from Fredericton down to Centreville which is nothing more than a branch line of, or a feeder for, the Canadian Pacific and over which no great amount of business can ever be hoped for because it simply goes through an agricultural country. It is as rich a country as you will find anywhere in Eastern Canada, but yet it cannot supply sufficient business in order that 40 per cent of it may pay the interest on $35,000 a mile because that is what the province will have to pay for the road. From Fredericton to Westfield, you would have somewhere about 60 miles of line. Let me ask my hon. friend what would be the proper proportion of a car of wheat from Winnipeg to St. John passing over that 60 miles of road and how much does he think 
that 60 miles would earn out of the 2,500 miles of road from Winnipeg to St. John. Why, Sir, if he had 25 cars a day during the whole year I do not believe he would have enough to pay the interest on this sixty miles of road to say nothing of the interest on the other eighty-seven miles from Fredericton north. While it may look rosy to him, and while his engineers may have painted a bright picture and may have made him believe that this connection from McGivney junction would be all that would be required, and would put the province in a position to pay this interest, all I have to say is that they do not know what they are talking about or that they have refrained from giving the minister the information. I am pointing out now the other side of it because, carrying out this present arangement, there are 87 miles costing $35,000 a mile and out of local business only the railway can never pay interest. Under this present arrangement 1 have no doubt that with the most favourable conditions the people of the province of New Brunswick will have to pay some $100,000 to $200,000 a year interest for all time to come. That is a very serious question and [DOT] I do not believe many hon. gentlemen on the other side realize what it does mean. It would not be very much for the province of Ontario, it would not be an awful burden to some of the western provinces having great resources, but it is a millstone around the neck of the people of New Brunswick which will be felt for all time to come. I wish the Minister of Public Works could realize this as we realise it because even now it is not too late to mend, to go back and carry out the original proposal. It is not too late to keep faith with the people of New Brunswick and try to relieve them from the awful financial burden that they see staring them in the face if this arrangement is carried out. Then my hon. friend says they are going to Westfield or, we say, to some other point on the Canadian Pacific. I do not think it makes very much difference because no matter whether they go to Westfield or whether they go to Wels-ford, it only means that the Canadian Pacific gets a little more of the freight rate. The main point is that if they get to 8t. John they are not going to1 have a through connection and they are not going to give us control of the through business originating in the western part of New Brunswick.

Mi. BOiGRIS: We have running rights over the Canadian Pacific.

You will get running
rights over the Canadian Pacfic, but as far as the people of New Brunswick are concerned, they will end when they get to Westfield.
That is only temporary.

I will give my hon.
friend credit for being sincere in making his statement, because I think he is absolutely sincere, but he does not know the conditions. You talk of building another road from Westfield to St. John paralleling the Canadian Pacific through those rock cuts. I do not know of a piece of railway in Eastern Canada that is any more expensive, or would be any more expensive to build, than paralleling the Canadian Pacific from Westfield to St. John.
The engineers say it can be done for $700,000 less than the other.

That is $50,000 a mile.
I do not believe it.
$
That covers the line from Gagetown to St. John.

They can build a line
from Gagetown to Westfield for $50,000 a mile, but to say that they can build it for $700,000' is absolute nonsense.
That is the report of the engineers.

You could not build that road from Westfield to St. John for $50,000 a mile. You could not build it for $60,000 a mile. If any hon. gentleman will keep in his mind what I am saying and the next time he goes to St. John over the Canadian Pacific, if he will just look out and see the kind of country through which he is travelling, the rock cuts and difficult country for the last ten or twelve miles before getting to St. John, he will realize that what I say is true. I do not care if all the engineers in the country would say so; our ordinary, common sense teaches us that these statements are absolutely untrue and impossible. When you come to cross the St. John river, it will cost $600,000 or $700,000 to bridge the St. John at its mouth. My hon. friend from St. John (Mr. Pugsley) stated a short time ago that the present bridge is inadequate. They have to rebuild the present Canadian Pacific bridge across the Falls. If the Government attempted to build another bridge across there and get a right of way from that bridge into the city of St. John, and to the Union Depot, $50,000 a mile, $100,000 a mile, $200,000 a mile would not pay for the cost of getting from that bridge into the Union Station. When they get to the Union depot, they are still some two or three miles from Courtenay Bay. The whole thing is impracticable, and when my hon. friends talk about it, they are talking about something which they know is not feasible, and which they know cannot be carried out. It simply means that they have decided to join on to the Canadian Pacific railway at Westfield and stop there. That is the end of the whole transaction. It is true that they may get running rights over the Canadian Pacific railway for a consideration, but they will be subjecting themselves to the control of the Canadian Pacific railway, and they will have to pay a pretty big percentage in order to get the Canadian Pacific railway to haul their freight over the fourteen miles. My hon. friends may think I am talking a little severely, but I know conditions down there; so does my hon. friend from St. John, and all our friends from New, Brunswick. I wish the hon. member for Charlotte (Mr. Hartt) were here. He knows conditions down there. So does the Minister of Marine and Fisheries. I see some of my Conservative friends from Nova Scotia opposite. They know conditions down there, if they would only speak up and say what they think of this fantastic story that the minister has been narrating, and which was prepared for him by somebody else this afternoon. It is the merest fantasy, with no foundation in fact whatever. The story is absolutely impossible. It simply comes down to this. There are only two schemes. One is to go to Westfield and stop there, and get the Canadian Pacific railway, to haul from there in; and the other is to cross the river farther up, by what is called the bridge route, and strike the Intercolonial railway at Rothesay, and from there go. to the terminals over their own tracks. Am I to understand from the statement and conclusions of the Minister of Public Works that if this extension to Vanceboro is ever built, it will have to be built by the local Government?
I did not say that it would be built to Vanceboro.

I will qualify that: either to Vanceboro or some other point on the American system of railways. But am I to understand that wherever it is built to

it will be built by the Government of New Brunswick, and not by the Dominion Government?
That is the proposal made by Mr. Gutelius. I do not know whether the Provincial Government has agreed uo it or not.

I want to be fair. I believe the minister told me some time ago that the New Brunswick Government had not accepted the proposal. We want the people of New Brunswick to know exactly what the proposal is, and exactly what the Government of New Brunswick is doing, because we have a lot of difficulty in ascertaining from the Government of New Brunswick the true condition of affairs. We have to adopt these methods in order to get information for the people of our province. That was our object in bringing this matter up, arid, I thank the Minister of Public Works fcir being so perfectly frank and honest about it. He has told the whole story, and now we should be able to send the Hanskrd down to our people in Fredericton, and they will know the stoTy exactly as it is. It is sometimes a great satisfaction to be able to come here and get evidence which has been denied to us at home.	,
My hon. friend referred to the fact that this road might be built from some point on the Valley railway, other than the point a few miles above Fredericton to Vance-boro. I have heard that idea discussed for the last eight or. ten years. The theory is that they would turn off somewhere near Meductic, twelve miles below Woodstock, then go in a southwesterly direction and strike the Maine Central either at Danforth, or possibly as far west as Mat-tawamkeag.
Bancroft.

They might possibly
strike it at Bancroft. But the route I have described is the story as 1 have heard it for the last six or eight years. In fact the Canadian Pacific Railway went so far as to have that line surveyed. I think it was surveyed up to Mattawamkeag. It may possibly be that their object in doing so was to get rid of utilizing any porti: n of the Maine Central. They have running rights from Mattawamkeag to Vanceboro, and they may have intended to go far enough west to eliminate any portion of the Maine Central system. But there is a great bend in the Maine Central railway, and I think the

nearest point would be Mattawamkeag, but whether Mattawamkeag, Bancroft or Danforth you would be compelled to build from 15 to 25 miles of railway through American territory. My hon. friend said this afternoon that the American railways were always out for business. Yes, they are, but I want to tell him that the Maine Central Railway is not out for building any more railways through that country, because there is another railway called the Bangor alnd Aroostook Railway, the majority of the stock of which we are generally led to believe is owned by the Maine Central, although the company is an entirely different entity. The country through which this road would run would not produce any business whatever. The Maine Central would never build a road through that country.
They would if they could get a lot of business.

They can get exactly the same business a't Vanceboro, and by getting it there, they get a longer haul. There is no use jn my hon. friend talking about the Maine Central building a railroad through that country. Why, if they did it would be a shorter haul for themselves, and they are not such gfeat idiots as to do that. So the gentlemen who have been putting up this story to my hon. friend and the Acting Minister of Railways, of making connections at Bancroft or Mattawamkeag with the American system of railways have simply been fooling them. There is nothing to it, and there never can be anything to it. And even Supposing the road was built you would be compelled to haul the freight of Nova Scotia and eastern New Brunswick fifty miles up along the Valley railway before turning it over to this new section. Therefore the whole thing is only a dream, something conjured up. I do not know whether it was conjured up by Mr. Gutelius as a reason for advising this Government to go back on their agreement with the people of New Brunswick, or whether it was conjured up by the Government of New Brunswick as a reason for their going back on their agreement. One is about as bad as the other, and I think it is just the tossing up of a copper whether this nonsensical scheme originated with Gutelius or with the Government. We believe this at least: That if i't is left td the Government of New Brunswick to build, it will never be built, and there will never be a,., harm in it.


There is just one other point, and I hope, Mr. Speaker, you will pardon me if I travel a little out of the line of answering my hon. friend's statements. It is a most remarkable thing to find a Conservative Government, not only of New Brunswick, but of Canada, taking to building more railways in order to get our produce to the United States.
More truck with the Yankees.

Why, these are the very gentlemen who were tearing their hair out four years ago for fear there would be more trade with the Yankees; the men who were waving the Old Flag about, who said that the lines of communication should be east and west, and not north and south; who said that we should not have any truck and trade with the Yankees, but should trade among ourselves; who said that the manufactured products of Ontario should be sent east to Nova Scotia and New Brunswick. That was the truly loyal way of carrying on the affairs of this country. And now these same people, in the space of four short years, are not simply advising, but compelling, or trying to compel-the New Brunswick Government to build a road at a cost of $1,500,000 in order that we may be able to trade with these despised Yankees. Truly, four years have wrought a wonderful change in the feelings of hon. gentlemen opposite. I congratulate them to this extent: that, if they are not sound on their , railway policy they are a great deal sounder on their trade policy than they were a few years ago, because, so far as we are concerned in my portion of Canada at least, we have no objection, whatever, to all the truck and trade with the Yankees that we can possibly have. It is in the United States that we sell a large part of our produce and where we try to make our money and we have no scruples whatever in trading there. They cannot make the trade too free and too easily accessible so far as we are concerned, but we do object to the expenditure of this $1,500,000 of our good money in order to help Mr. Gutelius work out his scheme or in order to help the Government of New , Brunswick out in their troubles with the people, because such a scheme is not necessary as we have now between the city of Fredericton and the American border all the railway communication that can possibly be required. As was pointed out by my hon. friend from Victoria (Mr. Michaud)
a little while ago, we have the Canadian Pacific railway running from Fredericton to Vanceboro; you go up sixty miles and there the Valley railway makes a connection with the Canadian Pacific railway which goes into the state of Maine again at a place called Houlton via Debec Junction. You go sixty miles above that and you come to another place where the railway could, if it came up to Andover, connect with the Canadian Pacific railway and go into the United States again.
Have you a connection at Woodstock?

Yes, the Valley railway connects with the Canadian Pacific railway, and the Canadian Pacific railway runs into the United States a few miles below Woodstock. Then you go up to Aroostook Junction and the Canadian Pacific railway connects there and runs into the state of Maine, and there is another connection between St. Leonards and Van Buren. With all these connections with the United States, it seems remarkable that my friends want the province of New Brunswick to spend $1,500,000 in order to have another connection paralleling the Canadian Pacific railway, but I hope the expenditure will not have to be made. I again thank my hon. friend the Minister of Public Works for his extreme courtesy' and honesty in giving us so much information, and I can only trust that tlfe resolution will carry and that the papers will be brought down before the close of the present session; in fact, if they are brought down within a week or ten days, it will be of great importance in discussing this matter when it comes up in the legislature of New Brunswick.
Motion agreed to.

speakeroldname: Mr. J. J. HUGHES (Kings, P. E. I.) moved:
speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this House, it is desirable that necessary action should be taken by the Government during this session to secure an amendment of the British North America Act so as to empower the Legislature of any province to prohibit the importation of intoxicating liquors into such province and the manufacture of such liquors within the province.
He said: Mr. Speaker, when the debate on this subject commenced the discussion was widened to include the resolution which stood on the Ordpr Paper in the name of the hon. member for Vancouver (Mr. COMMONS
Stevens), and also the resolution that stood in my name, because, although the resolutions were somewhat dissimilar, yet they referred to one subject, the prohibition or restriction of the consumption, sale and manufacture of intoxicating liquors, and they were, therefore, alike in certain particulars. The discussion the other day was taken part in by several hon. members, and the hon. member who moved the resolution and, the hon. member who seconded it spoke at considerable length. As it would be well, if possible, that as many members of this House as wish to take part in this discussion should have an opportunity of doing so, I will endeavour to make my remarks brief. There would really be no necessity of making lengthy remarks, because I do not think any argument is necessary to convince the great majority of hon. members of the desirability of legislation along the lines proposed, that is, to restrict, and, if possible, to prohibit the large consumption of alcoholic liquors in the Dominion of Canad,a.
Two speeches were made in opposition to the proposed legislation, one by the hon, member for North Waterloo (Mr. Weichel), who read an article which bore all the marks of having been prepared outside of Parliament by some person or persons interested in the liquor business. As it was, therefore, a megaphonic utterance, I do not think it is necessary to pay any further attention to it. There was, however, a speech delivered by the hon. member for St. Hyacinthe (Mr. Gauthier), which contained some original statements, if not original ideas, and, I think his speech ought to receive some consideration. The hon. member for St. Hyacinthe mentioned two countries in which the people were very temperate, but had other qualities that were very much to be deplored, and be wished the inference to be drawn that it was because the people of those countries were temperate that they were not otherwise desirable people. He instanced Turkey, saying that the Turks were very temperate, but that we should not imitate their habits and customs. I do not know much about the Turkish people, and I have not read much of their history; I have, however, spoken to some men who have travelled in Turkey and traded with the Turks, and I have been informed that, apart from their religion, which makes them consider it a meritorious deed, to shed the blood of a Christian, they are a pretty good people,

and that, for instance, the word of a Turkish merchant is as good as his bond.
His bond is all right.

Yes, his bond is all right, and, we have seen instances of Turkish magnanimity. It is recorded of them that at the Gallipoli peninsula they showed a magnanimity and a chivalry which the Austrians, or at least the Germans, have not shown in the great war that is now raging, but I am sure that the hon. member for St. Hyacinthe (Mr. Gauthier) would not suppose for a moment that the Turkish character would , be improved if they added intoxicating liquors to their national beverages.
Then, the hon. gentleman dwelt at some length upon the character of the Spanish people. His object was quite apparent. He said:
Spain, where hatred, where vendetta, where the bitterest passions of humanity are in full flame, is the most temperate country in the world.
I have read something about the character of the Spanish people. I have read books by English ladies and English .gentlemen who have travelled in Spain, who have lived in Spain, and know the character of the people, and who, not being of the same religious faith as the Spaniards, I suppose, would not be prejudiced in their favour. Yet these authors have borne testimony to the splendid character of these people in many respects. Of course, they have the warm southern blood, they are quickly excited to anger, and apt to resent an insult or injury, fancied or otherwise. Yet they are quick to forgive, and when they forgive they forget. But we are told concerning the Spanish people that they are hospitable to a degree, that their family life is pure and sound, and in many cases beautiful, and that they are not only temperate but honest-bars and locks are practically unknown in that country. In Spain the poor are not despised, nor is wealth worshipped. The beggar in the streets of Madrid, according to the books I have read, does not ask for alms in an abject or servile way, but as a brother in distress would ask his brother for help; and if he has to be refused, the man who refuses him apologizes for not being able to help his brother in distress. Should we not be justified in saying that the temperate habits of the people have much to do with their character in these respects? I think we should. Perhaps the hon. member for
